children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.recovery
children.doc:
What the data can recover, with an interval whose coverage is measured (#77).

A fitted parameter without an interval is a number with no claim attached, and an interval nobody has checked is a
claim with no evidence attached. This does both halves:

    >>> from pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.recovery import recover, coverage_study
    >>> result = recover(model, params, observations, level=0.95)     # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> result.interval("k").estimate, result.interval("k").lower, result.interval("k").upper   # doctest: +SKIP
    (0.81, 0.74, 0.89)

The interval is the linearised (Gauss-Newton) one from the Fisher information at the optimum, which is the interval the
data supports: ``J^T J`` with the noise the observations declare, plus the prior precision when a prior is given. The
same matrix answers the other question — **is this parameter identifiable at all?** — through
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.sensitivity.IdentifiabilityAnalyzer`, and a parameter the data cannot
separate from another is reported by name instead of being given a confident-looking interval.

``coverage_study`` is how the interval is checked: repeat a synthetic experiment with a known truth, count how often the
interval contains it, and compare with the level that was claimed. An interval that contains the truth 70 % of the time
while claiming 95 % is not a wide interval, it is a wrong one.

Both halves reuse what is already here: the standard deviation and the null space come from the same Fisher information
and the same reader that :mod:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.identifiability` uses (:func:`_std_from_F`,
:func:`_combination`), so the two cannot describe the same direction differently. ``interval="profile"`` swaps the
linearised interval for the profile-likelihood one, which is the honest choice when the model is visibly nonlinear.

classes.name: ParameterInterval
classes.doc: One recovered parameter with the interval the data supports at ``level``.

classes.name: RecoveryResult
classes.doc: The fit, the intervals, and what could not be recovered — the three things a discovery report needs.

classes.name: CoverageReport
classes.doc: How often the interval contained the truth, per parameter, against the level that was claimed.

methods.name: ci
methods.doc: Wilson interval of the coverage itself, so a rate of 0.93 from 20 runs is not read as 0.93.

methods.name: calibrations
methods.doc: ``under`` when the interval covers less than claimed, ``over`` when it is needlessly wide, else ``ok``.

functions.name: recover
functions.sig: (model: ForwardModel, params: ParameterSet, obs: Observations, *, level: float = 0.95, prior: Prior | None = None, free: Sequence[int] | None = None, interval: str = 'linear', analyzer: IdentifiabilityAnalyzer | None = None, **fit_kwargs) -> RecoveryResult
functions.doc:
Fit the free parameters and say, for each one, the interval the data supports and whether it is identifiable.

``level`` is the two-sided coverage of the interval. ``interval="linear"`` is the Gauss-Newton one — fast, and the
right shape when the model is close to linear over a standard deviation; ``"profile"`` re-fits the others over a
grid and takes the ``chi2_min + chi2_1(level)`` crossing, which stays honest when it is not. A parameter the data
cannot separate from another gets an infinite interval rather than a confident-looking one.

functions.name: coverage_study
functions.sig: (case: Callable[[np.random.Generator], tuple[Any, ParameterSet, Observations]], *, n: int = 200, level: float = 0.95, seed: int = 0, tolerance: float = 0.1, **recover_kwargs) -> CoverageReport
functions.doc:
Repeat a synthetic experiment with a known truth and count how often the interval contains it.

``case(rng)`` builds one experiment: it returns the model, the parameters (with ``truth`` set) and the
observations, whose values are already drawn at the truth with their declared noise. A case that draws its noise
from ``rng`` is what makes the repeats independent.

children.summary: What the data can recover, with an interval whose coverage is measured (#77).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.regularization
children.doc:
Regularization framework for inverse problems.

Provides differentiable regularization terms that penalise unphysical or
unlikely parameter values.  All regularizers accept PyTorch tensors so they
compose naturally with PINN physics losses.

Supported regularizers
----------------------
TikhonovRegularizer       R(θ) = λ ‖θ − θ₀‖²₂            (L2 / ridge)
SparsityRegularizer       R(θ) = λ ‖θ‖₁                  (L1 / LASSO)
TotalVariationRegularizer R(u) = λ TV(u)                  (anisotropic 1D/2D)
CompositeRegularizer      R(θ) = Σᵢ wᵢ Rᵢ(θ)
LCurveSelector            auto λ via L-curve + max curvature

References
----------
- Hansen (1992) "Analysis of Discrete Ill-Posed Problems by Means of the
  L-Curve"
- Vogel (2002) "Computational Methods for Inverse Problems"

classes.name: RegularizerBase
classes.doc: Abstract regularization term R(θ) → scalar loss.

methods.name: weight
methods.doc: Shorthand: scale this regularizer and return a composite.

classes.name: TikhonovRegularizer
classes.sig: (lambda_reg: float, prior: torch.Tensor | None = None, covariance: torch.Tensor | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Tikhonov / ridge regularizer: R(θ) = λ ‖θ − θ₀‖²₂.

Parameters
----------
lambda_reg : float
    Regularization strength λ > 0.
prior : torch.Tensor or None
    Prior mean θ₀.  Defaults to **zero** if None.
covariance : torch.Tensor or None
    Prior covariance C₀ (p×p).  If given, penalty becomes
    (θ−θ₀)^T C₀⁻¹ (θ−θ₀) (Mahalanobis distance).

classes.name: SparsityRegularizer
classes.sig: (lambda_reg: float, eps: float = 1e-06) -> None
classes.doc:
L1 / LASSO regularizer: R(θ) = λ ‖θ‖₁.

Promotes sparse parameter identification (many parameters near zero).
Uses a differentiable approximation near zero to avoid gradient issues.

Parameters
----------
lambda_reg : float
    Regularization strength.
eps : float
    Smoothing parameter for the L1 approximation `sqrt(θ² + ε²)`.
    Set to 0 for exact L1 (non-smooth at 0).

classes.name: TotalVariationRegularizer
classes.sig: (lambda_reg: float, eps: float = 1e-06) -> None
classes.doc:
Anisotropic Total Variation regularizer for spatial field parameters.

Supports:
- 1D field: θ ∈ R^n, TV(θ) = Σᵢ |θᵢ₊₁ − θᵢ|
- 2D field: θ ∈ R^{H×W}, TV(θ) = Σ |∂ₓθ| + |∂ᵧθ|

Parameters
----------
lambda_reg : float
eps : float
    Smooth approximation: |x| ≈ sqrt(x² + ε²).

classes.name: CompositeRegularizer
classes.sig: (terms: list[tuple[float, RegularizerBase]] | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Weighted sum of multiple regularizers: R(θ) = Σᵢ wᵢ Rᵢ(θ).

Parameters
----------
terms : list of (weight, RegularizerBase)

methods.name: add
methods.doc: Append a weighted regularizer in-place and return self.

classes.name: LCurveResult
classes.doc:
Result of an L-curve analysis.

Attributes
----------
lambdas : list of float
    Tested λ values.
data_misfits : list of float
    Data misfit ‖G(θ_λ) − y‖ for each λ.
regularization_norms : list of float
    ‖θ_λ − θ₀‖ for each λ.
optimal_lambda : float
    λ at the corner of the L-curve (maximum curvature point).
curvatures : list of float
    Discrete curvature estimate for each λ.

classes.name: LCurveSelector
classes.sig: (train_fn: Callable[[float], tuple[float, float]], lambdas: list[float] | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Automatic regularization parameter selection via the L-curve.

The L-curve plots ‖residual‖ vs ‖regularization norm‖ (log-log scale) for
a range of λ values.  The optimal λ is at the corner — the point of maximum
discrete curvature.

Parameters
----------
train_fn : callable(lambda_reg: float) -> (data_misfit: float, reg_norm: float)
    Function that trains the inverse problem with the given λ and returns
    the two L-curve coordinates.
lambdas : list of float, optional
    λ grid to search.  Defaults to 30 log-spaced values in [1e-6, 1e2].

Example
-------
>>> selector = LCurveSelector(lambda lam: train_and_eval(lam))
>>> result = selector.select()
>>> print(f"Optimal λ = {result.optimal_lambda:.2e}")

methods.name: select
methods.doc: Run the L-curve sweep and return the result.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.sbinn
children.doc:
Systems-biology informed neural networks (SBINN): parameters and hidden states of an ODE system from partial data.

Yazdani, Lu, Raissi and Karniadakis, PLoS Comput Biol 16(11):e1007575 (2020); the workflow as described by Daneker,
Zhang, Karniadakis and Lu, arXiv:2202.01723 (2022), section 4. Reimplemented here from that description (no code
copied) on any :class:`~pinneapple_physics.biology.ODESystem`:

* one network ``t -> x(t)`` for all states, with an input-scaling layer (``t / T``), a feature layer
  (``t~, sin(t~), ..., sin(K t~)`` with ``t~ = feature_scale * t``) and an output-scaling layer (each state times its
  magnitude);
* unknown parameters as trainable scalars mapped into their search range by ``lo + (hi - lo) (tanh(v) + 1) / 2``;
* loss ``L = L_data + L_ode + L_aux``: mean squared misfit to the observed states, mean squared ODE residual of every
  state at the collocation times, and the misfit of all states at two times (``aux_times``, e.g. the first and last
  measurement) when they are known. Every term is computed in units scaled by the state magnitudes and the time span,
  so the terms are of the same order without hand-tuned weights (``units="scaled"``), or in physical units with
  hand-set ``weights`` and per-state ``ode_weights`` as the paper's code does (``units="raw"``); the ODE term is the
  sum over states of each state's mean squared residual;
* training in two stages, as in the paper: data only (network fit, parameters frozen), then all terms with the
  parameters trainable. Adam throughout.

:class:`SBINNResult` keeps the inferred parameters, their history, the loss history and the network; ``predict``
evaluates the states. The inferred parameters should be re-checked by integrating the ODE with them
(:meth:`SBINNResult.forward_check`), which is what the trust report of an inference rests on.

methods.name: forward_check
methods.sig: (system, t, observed: Sequence[str] = (), data: Mapping[str, np.ndarray] | None = None, **simulate_kw) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Integrate ``system`` with the inferred parameters and compare with the data (relative L2 per observed
state) and with the network's own states (how far the network is from an ODE solution).

classes.name: SBINN
classes.sig: (system, unknown: Sequence[str], search_range: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], data: Mapping[str, tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]], *, t_collocation = None, aux: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None, aux_times: Sequence[float] = (), config: SBINNConfig | None = None)
classes.doc:
Infer ``unknown`` parameters of ``system`` (with their ``search_range``) from observations of some states.

``data`` maps an observed state (or ``<state>`` of the system) to ``(t, values)``; ``t_collocation`` are the ODE
residual times (default: the union of the data times); ``aux`` maps every state to its known values at
``aux_times`` (the paper's L_aux), or is None.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (verbose: bool = False, checkpoint: str | None = None, checkpoint_every: int = 10000, checkpoint_seconds: float = 300.0) -> SBINNResult
methods.doc:
Train. With ``checkpoint`` (a file path) the network, parameters, optimiser and history are saved every
``checkpoint_every`` epochs or ``checkpoint_seconds``, whichever comes first, and a run restarts from the file
when it exists (long runs survive restarts).

children.summary: Systems-biology informed neural networks (SBINN): parameters and hidden states of an ODE system from partial data.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.sensitivity
children.doc:
Sensitivity analysis for inverse problems.

Quantifies how sensitive the observables are to each physical parameter,
providing essential information for:
- Identifiability analysis (can parameters be recovered from available data?)
- Experimental design (which sensors / measurements are most informative?)
- Uncertainty propagation (which parameters drive output uncertainty?)
- Prioritizing regularization (ill-conditioned directions need stronger reg)

Three levels of analysis
------------------------
LocalSensitivity       Jacobian J = ∂G/∂θ at a nominal point; FIM = J^T J / σ²
IdentifiabilityAnalyzer FIM eigenanalysis; D/A/E-optimality criteria
GlobalSensitivity      Sobol variance-based indices via Saltelli's method

References
----------
- Saltelli et al. (2010) "Variance based sensitivity analysis of model output"
- Kaipio & Somersalo (2005) "Statistical and Computational Inverse Problems"
- Pukelsheim (1993) "Optimal Design of Experiments" (D/A/E-optimality)

classes.name: LocalSensitivityResult
classes.doc:
Results of local sensitivity analysis.

Attributes
----------
jacobian : np.ndarray, shape (k, p)
    J = ∂G/∂θ at the nominal parameter values.
fisher_information : np.ndarray, shape (p, p)
    FIM = J^T Γ⁻¹ J.
singular_values : np.ndarray, shape (min(k,p),)
    Singular values of J.
sensitivity_indices : np.ndarray, shape (p,)
    Per-parameter sensitivity: ‖Jᵢ‖ / ‖J‖_F  (column norms).
param_names : list of str
    Names of the parameters in order.

classes.name: LocalSensitivity
classes.sig: (forward_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor], noise_std: float = 1.0, param_names: list[str] | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Local (linearized) sensitivity analysis around a nominal parameter point.

Computes the Jacobian J = ∂G/∂θ using PyTorch's reverse-mode AD, then
derives the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for parameter identifiability.

Parameters
----------
forward_fn : callable(theta: Tensor) -> Tensor
    Maps parameter vector θ ∈ R^p to observable vector G(θ) ∈ R^k.
noise_std : float or np.ndarray
    Observation noise standard deviation (scalar or (k,) array).
    Used to form Γ⁻¹ = diag(1/σ²) in the FIM.
param_names : list of str, optional
    Names of the p parameters (for reporting).

methods.name: compute
methods.doc: Compute local sensitivity at ``theta_nominal``.

methods.name: finite_difference_jacobian
methods.doc: Finite-difference Jacobian (fallback; no autograd required).

classes.name: IdentifiabilityResult
classes.doc:
Output of identifiability analysis.

Attributes
----------
eigenvalues : np.ndarray, shape (p,)
    Eigenvalues of FIM, ascending order.
eigenvectors : np.ndarray, shape (p, p)
    Columns = eigenvectors of FIM.
condition_number : float
    κ(FIM) = λ_max / λ_min (large → ill-conditioned).
d_optimality : float
    det(FIM) — larger is better (D-optimal design criterion). Exactly 0
    for a rank-deficient / partially non-identifiable FIM.
pseudo_d_optimality : float
    Product of the strictly-positive eigenvalues only, i.e. det(FIM)
    restricted to the identifiable subspace. Can be nonzero even when
    ``d_optimality`` is 0, but does *not* by itself signal full
    identifiability — check ``unidentifiable_indices`` for that.
a_optimality : float
    trace(FIM⁻¹) — smaller is better (A-optimal).
e_optimality : float
    λ_min(FIM) — larger is better (E-optimal).
identifiable_indices : list of int
    Indices of *identifiable* parameters (eigenvalue > tol).
unidentifiable_indices : list of int
    Indices of parameters that cannot be recovered from the data.
param_names : list of str

classes.name: IdentifiabilityAnalyzer
classes.sig: (tol: float = 1e-06) -> None
classes.doc:
Analyse parameter identifiability from the Fisher Information Matrix.

Parameters
----------
tol : float
    Eigenvalue threshold: parameters with eigenvalue < tol · λ_max are
    considered unidentifiable (zero in effective rank sense).

methods.name: analyze
methods.sig: (fim: np.ndarray, param_names: list[str] | None = None) -> IdentifiabilityResult
methods.doc: Perform identifiability analysis on a Fisher Information Matrix.

methods.name: effective_rank
methods.doc: Number of identifiable parameters (eigenvalues above threshold).

classes.name: SobolResult
classes.doc:
Sobol sensitivity indices.

Attributes
----------
S1 : np.ndarray, shape (p,)
    First-order (main effect) indices: fraction of variance explained by θᵢ alone.
ST : np.ndarray, shape (p,)
    Total effect indices: fraction including all interactions with θᵢ.
param_names : list of str
n_samples : int
    Number of Monte Carlo samples used.

classes.name: GlobalSensitivity
classes.sig: (forward_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], param_bounds: list[tuple[float, float]], n_samples: int = 1024, seed: int | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Variance-based global sensitivity analysis (Sobol indices).

Uses Saltelli's (2010) estimator with two random matrices A, B.

Parameters
----------
forward_fn : callable(theta_batch: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
    Vectorized forward model; input (N, p), output (N,) or (N, k).
    If output is (N, k), Sobol indices are averaged over outputs.
param_bounds : list of (lo, hi)
    Uniform prior bounds for each parameter.
n_samples : int
    Base sample count N.  Total evaluations = N * (2 + 2p): N for A, N
    for B, and N each for AB_i and BA_i per parameter (both AB_i and
    BA_i are used, averaged together for a lower-variance estimate).
seed : int, optional

methods.name: compute
methods.doc: Run Sobol analysis and return indices.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.solver
children.doc:
High-level InverseProblemSolver combining all inverse-problem components.

Wires together:
- A physics model (PINN or any nn.Module)
- Observation operator H
- Data-misfit / noise model D
- Regularization R
- Optimizer choice: gradient-based (Adam / L-BFGS) or derivative-free (EKI)

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.solver import InverseProblemSolver, InverseSolverConfig
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.noise_models import HuberMisfit
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.regularization import TikhonovRegularizer
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.obs_operator import PointObsOperator

>>> cfg = InverseSolverConfig(method="adam", n_iters=2000, lr=5e-4)
>>> solver = InverseProblemSolver(
...     model=pinn,
...     obs_operator=PointObsOperator(sensor_locs),
...     data_misfit=HuberMisfit(delta=0.5),
...     regularizer=TikhonovRegularizer(lambda_reg=1e-3),
...     config=cfg,
... )
>>> result = solver.solve(y_obs, theta_init)
>>> print(result.theta_opt, result.final_misfit)

classes.name: InverseSolverConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for InverseProblemSolver.

Parameters
----------

    Optimisation method:
    - "adam"   — gradient-based, Adam optimiser.
    - "lbfgs"  — gradient-based, L-BFGS (good for few parameters).
    - "eki"    — derivative-free Ensemble Kalman Inversion.
    - "teki"   — derivative-free Tikhonov-regularised EKI.
n_iters : int
    Gradient iterations (adam/lbfgs) or EKI update steps.
lr : float
    Learning rate (adam only).
lbfgs_max_iter : int
    Inner iterations per L-BFGS step.
device : str
grad_clip : float
    Gradient clip norm (0 = disabled).
print_every : int
    Print progress every N iterations (0 = silent).
# EKI-specific
eki_n_ensemble : int
    Ensemble size for EKI/TEKI.
eki_noise_std : float
    Observation noise std for EKI.
eki_lambda_reg : float
    Tikhonov weight for TEKI.
eki_init_spread : float
    Ensemble spread initialisation.
seed : int, optional

classes.doc:
Result of an inverse problem solve.

Attributes

    Optimal parameters.  If ``theta_init`` was a ``nn.ParameterDict``,
    returns a dict of numpy arrays.

classes.sig: (model: nn.Module, obs_operator: ObsOperatorBase, data_misfit: DataMisfitBase | None = None, regularizer: RegularizerBase | None = None, config: InverseSolverConfig | None = None, extra_loss_fn: Callable | None = None) -> None

Unified solver for physics-informed inverse problems.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.structural
children.doc:
Identify the parameters of a structure from displacements measured at a few points (#177, item S28).

The engineering question is the everyday one: a load was applied to a cantilever, a dial gauge or an LVDT
recorded the deflection at a few stations, and the question is what the beam was made of and how hard it
was pushed. This module answers it with the machinery already in
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems`: a forward model (:class:`~.forward.CallableModel` wrapping
Timoshenko beam theory, or CalculiX itself), :func:`~.recovery.recover` for the fit and the intervals, and
:func:`~.identifiability.analyze_identifiability` for the question that decides whether the intervals mean
anything.

The answer nobody expects: E and P cannot both be identified from displacements
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For a cantilever the deflection is ``w(x) = P f(x) / E`` -- linear in the load and linear in the
compliance. Displacements at any number of stations, at **one** load level, therefore see the ratio
``P/E`` and nothing else: doubling E and doubling P leaves every measured number identical. The
identifiability analysis reports it as a dead direction, and :func:`identify_cantilever` refuses to quote
two confident intervals for a pair the data only see as a product. What makes them separable is
information the displacements do not carry: a load cell (``unknown="modulus"``), a material certificate
(``unknown="load"``), or measurements at two different load levels.

What is measured, and what the uncertainty is
----------------------------------------------
The synthetic data come from **CalculiX** (a C3D20R brick cantilever, the case validated in
``tests/test_calculix_bridge.py``), and the forward model used for the inversion is the Timoshenko beam.
Those are not the same model: the 3-D element carries shear, Poisson effects and the local deformation
under the load, which the beam formula only approximates, and the gap measured at the four stations of the
reference case is 3.3 %. Rather than pretend otherwise, the observation
noise handed to the inversion carries the measured model-form gap as a second term
(``sigma = sqrt(sigma_noise^2 + (model_form * |w|)^2)``), which is the ASME V&V 20 practice: a beam model
that claims 0.1 % accuracy against a 3-D solid would give an interval that is confidently wrong, and the
truth would fall outside it.

References
----------
* Timoshenko, S., *Strength of Materials*, 3rd ed., Van Nostrand, 1955 -- the deflection with shear.
* Roache, P.J., *Verification and Validation in Computational Science and Engineering*, Hermosa, 1998;
  ASME V&V 20-2009 -- numerical, input and model-form uncertainty as one budget.
* Raue, A. et al., "Structural and practical identifiability analysis of partially observed dynamical
  models", *Bioinformatics* 25(15), 2009 -- the profile-likelihood and dead-direction reading used by
  ``inverse_problems.identifiability``.

classes.name: ObservationSet
classes.sig: (*, stations: np.ndarray, measured: np.ndarray, sigma: np.ndarray, truth: np.ndarray, noise: float, model_form: float, truth_parameters: dict[str, float]) -> None
classes.doc: A set of gauge readings: the stations, what they read, and the sigma each reading carries.

methods.name: observations
methods.doc: The same readings in the form :func:`~.recovery.recover` takes.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form (this is what the CalculiX run is stored as).

classes.name: Identification
classes.doc: One identification run: the fit, the parameters it fitted, and the two questions it has to answer.

methods.name: verdict
methods.doc: Did it come back, and could it have?

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form.

functions.name: timoshenko_deflection
functions.sig: (x: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, *, E: float, P: float, L: float = GEOMETRY['L'], b: float = GEOMETRY['b'], h: float = GEOMETRY['h'], nu: float = GEOMETRY['nu']) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Deflection of a cantilever under a tip load, with the shear term:
``w(x) = P x^2 (3L - x) / (6 E I) + P x / (kappa G A)``, ``I = b h^3 / 12``, ``kappa = 5/6``.

The second term is why this model is closer to the 3-D solid than Euler-Bernoulli: at ``L/h = 10``
shear carries 0.8 % of the tip deflection, and a model that omitted it would put that 0.8 % into the
recovered modulus.

functions.name: timoshenko_model
functions.sig: (*, stations: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, L: float = GEOMETRY['L'], b: float = GEOMETRY['b'], h: float = GEOMETRY['h'], nu: float = GEOMETRY['nu'], E: float, P: float) -> CallableModel
functions.doc:
The forward model the inversion calls: Timoshenko deflection at ``stations`` from ``(E, P)``.

``E`` and ``P`` are the analysis point (the initial guess of an estimation), the same convention the
rest of :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems` uses.

functions.name: cantilever_measurements
functions.sig: (*, E: float, P: float, stations: Sequence[float], noise: float, model_form: float, L: float = GEOMETRY['L'], b: float = GEOMETRY['b'], h: float = GEOMETRY['h'], nu: float = GEOMETRY['nu'], seed: int = 0) -> ObservationSet
functions.doc:
Synthetic displacements at ``stations``, with the noise and the model-form gap declared separately.

``noise`` is the gauge resolution in metres (an LVDT is micrometres); ``model_form`` is the measured
relative gap between the 3-D solver and the beam formula, folded into the sigma the inversion is given
so that a bias the model cannot represent widens the interval instead of displacing it silently.

functions.name: load_measurements
functions.sig: (path: str | Path | None = None) -> ObservationSet
functions.doc: The displacements measured by CalculiX and stored with the tests, so this runs without the solver.

functions.name: identify_cantilever
functions.sig: (measurements: ObservationSet, *, unknown: str = 'modulus', guess: dict[str, float] | None = None, interval: str = 'profile') -> Identification
functions.doc:
Recover the unknown parameter(s) and return the fit, the intervals and the identifiability analysis.

``unknown`` is what the experiment does **not** know:

``"modulus"``
    the load is on a load cell and the material is unknown (``E`` free, ``P`` fixed);
``"load"``
    the material is certified and the actuator force is not (``P`` free, ``E`` fixed);
``"both"``
    neither is known. The fit runs, and the result carries the dead direction that says only ``P/E`` is
    identifiable -- an infinite interval per parameter rather than two confident-looking numbers.

``guess`` starts the fit away from the truth on purpose: passing the true values would make every
``recover`` look good.

children.summary: Identify the parameters of a structure from displacements measured at a few points (#177, item S28).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.studio
children.doc:
One interface to formulate an inverse problem, solve it with several methods and validate the answers.

An :class:`InverseProblem` is a forward model, the unknown parameters (scalars or the zones of a field), the
measurements, optional held-out measurements and, in synthetic studies, the known truth. :func:`solve_inverse`
runs one method; :func:`compare_methods` runs several on the *same* data and ranks them by held-out error.

=================  ===============================================================================================
``least_squares``  classical weighted least squares (trust-region reflective in scaled parameters); Jacobian from
                   the model's own sensitivities, autograd or central differences; Gauss-Newton intervals.
``adjoint``        L-BFGS-B on the misfit with the gradient from one adjoint solve (models with
                   ``adjoint_gradient``, e.g. :class:`~.models.RodModel`): the cost does not grow with the number
                   of unknowns, which is what makes field reconstruction affordable.
``autodiff``       L-BFGS-B with the gradient by PyTorch automatic differentiation through the model
                   (``predict_torch``).
``bayesian``       MAP with a Gaussian prior on the scaled parameters (and a smoothness prior on field zones:
                   Tikhonov regularisation), Laplace covariance, and an adaptive-Metropolis posterior when the
                   model is cheap.
``pinn``           a physics-informed network that learns the field and the unknown together (models with
                   ``pinn``: the Inverse Heat Lab fin and plate).
=================  ===============================================================================================

Every solution carries the estimates, their uncertainty when the method gives one, the reconstructed fields, the
residuals, the fit and held-out metrics, and, when the truth is known, the parameter and field errors and whether
the truth lies inside the stated interval. The identifiability report (``identifiability.py``) is computed once per
problem (at the least-squares fit: the Fisher information is local) and attached, so a method's answer for a
non-identifiable parameter is flagged instead of trusted.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.workflow
children.doc:
The standard inverse-modeling / parameter-discovery workflow (#1189): identifiability before the fit, estimation,
intervals, and the checks that say whether the estimate can be trusted.

The forward model is a library tool (or a callable) with keyword inputs: the measured conditions (columns of the
measurements), the parameters to find (``parameters``: name -> ``{lower, upper, initial}``) and fixed values.

1. **Identifiability first** (:func:`.identifiability.analyze_identifiability` at the initial guess, on the
   conditions of the measurements): the Fisher information's rank and conditioning, the parameter combinations the
   data cannot separate (named), and the D-optimal next measurements among ``candidates``. A structurally
   non-identifiable parameter is reported, never estimated.
2. **Estimation** (:func:`.calibration.calibrate`): least squares in log space for positive parameters, with
   ``holdout_fraction`` rows never used in the fit, bootstrap and Jacobian intervals.
3. **Checks**: reduced chi-square against the stated noise; the held-out rows; residual whiteness (Wald-Wolfowitz
   runs test of the residual signs, in the order of the first condition); no estimate at its bound; and a
   **synthetic recovery**: data generated at the estimate with the stated noise, refitted ``n_recovery`` times,
   must give intervals that cover the estimate at about their nominal rate.

children.doc:
pinneapple_inverse — Inverse Problems module for PINNeAPPle.

Provides a complete toolkit for physics-informed inverse problems:

Core components
---------------
Noise models (data-misfit terms):
  GaussianMisfit            standard L2 / Mahalanobis distance
  HuberMisfit               robust to moderate outliers
  CauchyMisfit              heavy-tailed; very robust
  StudentTMisfit            Student-t likelihood (controls tail weight)
  HeteroscedasticMisfit     per-observation noise variance

Regularization:
  TikhonovRegularizer       L2 ‖θ − θ₀‖², Mahalanobis variant
  SparsityRegularizer       L1 ‖θ‖₁ (smooth approximation)
  TotalVariationRegularizer TV(u) for spatial field parameters
  CompositeRegularizer      weighted sum of multiple regularizers
  LCurveSelector            automatic λ via L-curve + max curvature

Observation operators:
  PointObsOperator          evaluate u at sparse sensor locations
  LinearObsOperator         y = A u (projections, Radon, …)
  IntegralObsOperator       y = ∫ k(x) u(x) dx
  ComposedObsOperator       stack multiple operators

Sensitivity analysis:
  LocalSensitivity          Jacobian J = ∂G/∂θ; FIM = J^T Γ⁻¹ J
  IdentifiabilityAnalyzer   eigenanalysis of FIM; D/A/E-optimality
  GlobalSensitivity         Sobol variance-based indices (Saltelli method)

Derivative-free inversion:
  EnsembleKalmanInversion   standard EKI (Iglesias et al. 2013)
  IteratedEKI               Tikhonov-regularized EKI / TEKI (Chada et al. 2020)

High-level solver:
  InverseProblemSolver      wires all components; supports Adam / L-BFGS / EKI

Quick start
-----------
>>> import pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems as pinv
>>> import torch

>>> # Define forward model (PINN)
>>> from pinneapple_neural.architectures import ModelRegistry
>>> model = ModelRegistry.build("VanillaPINN", in_dim=2, out_dim=1)

>>> # Observation operator: evaluate at 50 sensor points
>>> sensor_locs = torch.rand(50, 2)
>>> H = pinv.PointObsOperator(sensor_locs)

>>> # Noise model
>>> D = pinv.HuberMisfit(delta=0.3, noise_std=0.02)

>>> # Regularizer
>>> R = pinv.TikhonovRegularizer(lambda_reg=1e-3)

>>> # Solver
>>> cfg = pinv.InverseSolverConfig(method="adam", n_iters=2000, lr=5e-4)
>>> solver = pinv.InverseProblemSolver(model, H, D, R, cfg)

>>> # Synthetic observations
>>> y_obs = H(model, sensor_locs).detach() + 0.02 * torch.randn(50, 1)

>>> # Solve
>>> result = solver.solve(y_obs, sensor_locs)
>>> print(f"Final misfit: {result.final_misfit:.4e}")

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.linalg
children.doc:
One linear-algebra layer for the library: operators, spectra, POD and conditioning (X18, #202).

``pinneapple_analysis.numerics.linalg`` (#1061) answers "where did my digits go?" for a dense matrix. What the
library was missing is the layer above it -- the one a surrogate, a reduced-order model or a sensitivity
study actually calls:

``LinearOperator``
    A shape, a ``matvec`` and (when it is given) an ``rmatvec``. Everything else in this module takes either
    a matrix or an operator, so a solver wrapped as a callable and a matrix on disk are the same argument.
    The adjoint is never invented: an operator built without ``rmatvec`` refuses ``.adjoint()`` instead of
    returning its transpose, which is the wrong answer when the operator is not symmetric.
``pod``
    Proper orthogonal decomposition by SVD, with the energy captured, the rank the energy asked for, the
    coefficients and the reconstruction error **measured** on the snapshots that produced the basis.
``modal_analysis``
    Eigenvalues, frequencies, damping ratios, mode shapes and modal participation, plus the condition
    number of the eigenvector basis, which is what says whether those eigenvalues can be quoted at all.
    For a :class:`LinearOperator` the modes are Ritz values from the Krylov subspace, and the residual
    ``||A v - lambda v||`` is reported so the approximation is not mistaken for the exact spectrum.
``arnoldi``
    The Krylov basis and the Hessenberg matrix behind it, for a matrix or an operator.
``condition_estimate``
    The Hager-Higham 1-norm estimator: a lower bound on ``||A||_1 ||A^-1||_1`` from a handful of solves,
    which is the only affordable answer for a matrix-free operator. When the exact value is available (a
    dense matrix) both are returned, so the estimate is reported against the number it approximates.
``adjoint_sensitivity``
    ``d(c^T x)/dp`` for ``A(p) x = b(p)`` by one adjoint solve instead of one solve per parameter, with
    each value checked against a central difference of the re-solved system.

What is not here
----------------
No sparse storage, no parallel or distributed operators, no iterative solvers of its own (those live in
``numerics.linalg``: ``conjugate_gradient``, ``gmres``, ``bicgstab``), no Galerkin projection (that is
``pinneapple_analysis.reduced_order``, which builds the ROM operators this module's ``pod`` supplies the
basis for), and no autodiff: the sensitivity here is a linear-adjoint statement about a matrix, not a
backpropagation through a network (``pinneapple_core.operators`` does that). The condition estimator is
the 1-norm one; a 2-norm estimate would need a spectral norm estimator, and is not written.

Design rules
------------
* **Measured, not claimed.** The POD reconstruction error, the modal residual and the estimator's gap to
  the exact condition number are all returned next to the object they describe.
* **Refusals are explicit.** An operator with no adjoint refuses the adjoint; a non-square matrix refuses
  eigen analysis; a defective matrix says its eigenvalues are ill-conditioned instead of quoting them.
* **numpy in, numpy out.** Every function takes and returns numpy arrays or dataclasses with ``to_dict``;
  no torch, no I/O.

References
----------
* Trefethen, L.N. and Bau, D., *Numerical Linear Algebra*, SIAM, 1997 -- the Krylov/Ritz reading of a
  spectrum and the conditioning of an eigenvector basis.
* Golub, G.H. and Van Loan, C.F., *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins, 2013 -- POD, the SVD and
  modal decomposition.
* Hager, W.W., "Condition estimates", *SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput.* 5(2), 1984; Higham, N.J., "FORTRAN
  subroutines for estimating the 1-norm of a matrix", *ACM TOMS* 14(2), 1988 -- the estimator LAPACK uses
  (``dlacn2``).
* Sirovich, L., "Turbulence and the dynamics of coherent structures", *Quart. Appl. Math.* 45, 1987 -- POD.
* Giles, M.B. and Pierce, N.A., "An introduction to the adjoint approach to design", *Flow, Turbulence and
  Combustion* 65, 2000 -- the adjoint sensitivity.

classes.name: LinearOperator
classes.sig: (matvec: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], shape: tuple[int, int], *, rmatvec: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None, name: str = 'A') -> None
classes.doc:
A linear map with a shape: ``matvec``, and ``rmatvec`` when the adjoint is known.

The point of the class is that every function here can take a matrix or this, without the caller
building ``N x N`` dense storage for an operator that is a function. The shape is ``(m, n)`` for a map
from ``R^n`` to ``R^m``; a vector comes in and out as a ``float64`` numpy array.

    >>> A = LinearOperator(lambda x: 2.0 * x, (3, 3), rmatvec=lambda y: 2.0 * y)
    >>> A.to_dense()
    array([[2., 0., 0.],
           [0., 2., 0.],
           [0., 0., 2.]])

functions.name: pod
functions.sig: (snapshots: np.ndarray, *, energy: float = 0.999, rank: int | None = None, subtract_mean: bool = True) -> PODResult
functions.doc:
Proper orthogonal decomposition: the optimal linear basis for ``snapshots``, by SVD.

``snapshots`` is ``(n, m)`` -- one snapshot per **column**, which is the convention of
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.reduced_order` and of the POD literature. The rank is the smallest one whose
cumulative energy reaches ``energy``, or ``rank`` when it is given, capped by the **numerical rank** of
the data: a singular value at the rounding level of the data is a zero with a sign, so asking for ten
modes of a one-mode dataset returns one rather than nine columns of noise.

The reconstruction error is measured on the snapshots and returned: a basis that captures 99.9 % of the
energy and reconstructs the data to 1e-2 has told you something the energy number alone did not. It is
the *relative* Frobenius error against ``||X||``, so with the mean removed it equals
``sqrt(1 - energy_captured) * ||X - mean|| / ||X||`` -- which is Eckart-Young with the mean taken out.

functions.name: arnoldi
functions.sig: (A: LinearOperator | np.ndarray, b: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, m: int | None = None, *, tol: float = 1e-12) -> Arnoldi
functions.doc:
Arnoldi iteration: ``K_m(A, b) = span{b, Ab, ..., A^{m-1}b}`` and ``A V_m = V_{m+1} H``.

The Ritz values -- the eigenvalues of ``H_m`` -- are the best approximation to the spectrum that this
subspace can see, and the residual of each is ``|h_{m+1,m}| * |last component of its eigenvector|``,
which is what says whether the approximation has converged. A breakdown (``h = 0``) means the subspace
is invariant and the Ritz values are then **exact**, which is why ``breakdown`` is reported rather than
treated as a failure.

functions.name: modal_analysis
functions.sig: (A: LinearOperator | np.ndarray, *, krylov: int | None = None, frequencies_in_hz: bool = True) -> ModalAnalysis
functions.doc:
Eigenvalues, frequencies, damping ratios, mode shapes and participation of ``A``.

A dense matrix is diagonalised exactly (``n x n``), and with it the **left** eigenvectors are available,
so the participation factor ``|phi_i^H psi_i| / (||phi_i|| ||psi_i||)`` -- how much mode ``i`` is
excited by a generic input -- is measured, and the condition number of the eigenvector basis says how
far the eigenvalues can move under a perturbation of the matrix. A near-defective matrix (that
condition above ``1e8``) gets ``LINALG.NEAR_DEFECTIVE``: its eigenvalues are the ill-conditioned
quantity, not its eigenvectors.

A :class:`LinearOperator` has no dense diagonalisation to run, so the modes are **Ritz values** from
:func:`arnoldi` with ``krylov`` steps; ``ritz_approximation`` is then ``True`` and every mode reports
its measured residual ``||A v - lambda v||``. Reading a Ritz value as an eigenvalue is the classic way
to publish a mode that does not exist, so the flag travels with the result.

``frequency`` is ``|Im lambda| / 2pi`` when ``frequencies_in_hz``, and ``|Im lambda|`` (the angular
rate) otherwise; ``damping_ratio`` is ``-Re lambda / |lambda|``, which is the usual
``zeta = 1`` for a real stable eigenvalue and ``0`` for an undamped oscillation.

functions.name: condition_estimate
functions.sig: (A: LinearOperator | np.ndarray, solve: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None, *, solve_adjoint: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None, max_iter: int = 5, exact: bool | None = None) -> ConditionEstimate
functions.doc:
``||A||_1 * ||A^-1||_1`` by the Hager-Higham estimator: a lower bound from a few solves.

``solve`` must compute ``A^-1 r``; for a matrix it defaults to ``np.linalg.solve`` and the exact 2-norm
condition number is reported alongside. For a matrix-free operator, pass the solver -- the estimator is
then the only affordable answer. It is a **lower bound** on ``||A^-1||_1``, so a lower bound on the
condition number: it can miss a large value, it cannot invent one.

The iteration is Hager's: with ``B = A^-1`` and ``x = 1/n``, compute ``y = B x``, take ``xi = sign(y)``,
``z = B^T xi`` (one transposed solve), move ``x`` to the unit vector of ``argmax |z|``, and repeat until
the estimate stops growing or the sign vector has been found. The ``||A||_1`` factor is the maximum
column sum, measured with one application of the operator per column.

``solve_adjoint`` (computing ``A^-T r``) is what makes the transposed step possible. It defaults to the
transpose of a dense matrix; for a matrix-free operator it must be given, and without it the estimate
comes from the single right-hand side ``1/n`` -- still a valid lower bound, weaker, and ``iterations``
says ``1`` so the caller can tell the two apart.

functions.name: adjoint_sensitivity
functions.sig: (A: LinearOperator | np.ndarray, b: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, output: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, deriv_A: Sequence[np.ndarray] | np.ndarray | None = None, deriv_b: Sequence[Sequence[float]] | np.ndarray | None = None, *, step: float = 1e-06) -> SensitivityResult
functions.doc:
``d(c^T x)/dp`` where ``A(p) x = b(p)``, by the adjoint method, with a finite-difference check.

For each parameter ``p_k`` with ``dA_k = dA/dp_k`` and ``db_k = db/dp_k``::

    dJ/dp_k = lambda^T (db_k - dA_k x),     with   A^T lambda = c

One factorization of ``A`` and one of ``A^T`` gives every parameter at once, against ``x`` solved once --
which is the whole point when there are many parameters and few outputs. ``checked`` is the same
derivative from a central difference of the re-solved system at ``+/- step``: the two should agree, and
``relative_error`` is the measured gap. A large gap is reported, not hidden, because the adjoint formula
is exact and a disagreement means the derivatives supplied do not match the operator.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.multifidelity_workflow
children.doc:
Two data levels in one workflow: the cheap model everywhere, the expensive solver where it pays (#35).

The pieces were already here and each one answered its own question. :class:`pinneapple_data.co_kriging.CoKriging`
fits the Kennedy-O'Hagan model ``z_high = rho * z_low + delta`` with the discrepancy learned rather than assumed;
:func:`pinneapple_data.co_kriging.study` measures what that buys over a single-fidelity Gaussian process at the same
count of expensive runs; :class:`pinneapple_data.multifidelity.FidelityPair` pairs the two levels of a table; and
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.fidelity.serve` turns a surrogate into a route, answering each request with the model or
with the solver and writing down why.

What was missing is the **workflow**: one object that takes the two levels as the *functions they are*, spends a
budget on them, and answers the question a study is actually for -- *does the cheap level pay for itself?* -- with a
number instead of a preference. :class:`MultiFidelityWorkflow` is that object:

* the expensive designs are a **nested subset** of the cheap ones (:meth:`FidelityPlan.designs`), so every expensive
  run has a cheap value at the same design and the discrepancy is measured rather than interpolated;
* two models are fitted on the same data -- the co-kriging model and a single-fidelity Gaussian process on the
  expensive runs alone -- and both are scored when an oracle is given;
* the comparison is made at **equal cost**, which is the only comparison that decides anything. One expensive run
  costs ``1 / cost_ratio`` cheap ones, so a plan with ``n_high`` expensive and ``n_low`` cheap runs has spent
  ``n_high + cost_ratio * n_low`` expensive-run equivalents, and the honest baseline is a single-fidelity GP given
  *that* many expensive runs. Comparing against a GP with only ``n_high`` runs flatters co-kriging by handing it free
  information;
* the verdict is stated as a **break-even**: the largest ``cost_ratio`` at which the cheap level still pays. Above it
  the workflow says the multi-fidelity model does not pay and the budget belongs to the expensive level;
* :meth:`MultiFidelityRun.serves` puts the fitted model behind :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.fidelity.serve` with the
  expensive level as the escalation solver, so what the workflow fits is what a service answers with.

The measured case, and the number that does not flatter
------------------------------------------------------
:func:`rod_fidelities` is a real pair of solvers: the same one-dimensional Poisson problem solved by ``fem`` at two
mesh resolutions -- the coarse case is the cheap level, the fine one the expensive level -- and the quantity of
interest is the peak of the field. Measured on this machine (``2026-11-25``), 10 expensive designs, 64 cheap ones and
120 held-out expensive designs scored against a ten-times-finer solve:

==========================  ==============================  ==============
model                     relative error on held-out designs gain
==========================  ==============================  ==============
co-kriging, 10 + 64       7.8e-2                           --
high-fidelity only, 10    1.8e-1                           2.28 x
high-fidelity only, 11    1.1e-1                           1.36 x
high-fidelity only, 12    5.7e-2                           0.74 x
==========================  ==============================  ==============

So the cheap level more than doubles the accuracy at the same number of expensive runs, and it **stops paying once two
more expensive runs are on the table**: the break-even is one extra expensive run, a cost ratio of 1/64 = 0.016, i.e.
one expensive run has to cost more than about sixty coarse ones for the coarse runs to be worth buying. A coarse 2-D
CFD case against a fine one is well inside that; refining a mesh by a factor of two is not, and the workflow says so.
Both numbers are asserted in ``tests/test_multifidelity_workflow.py``; the docstring of
:func:`benchmark_multifidelity_workflow` carries the table the benchmark prints.

classes.name: FidelityPlan
classes.doc:
How the two levels are paid for.

``n_high`` expensive runs and ``n_low`` cheap ones, with ``cost_ratio`` = what one cheap run costs as a fraction
of one expensive run (``0.02`` says a coarse case is 1/50 of a fine one). ``total_cost`` is the plan in
expensive-run equivalents -- the only currency in which the two models can be compared.

methods.name: total_cost
methods.doc: The plan in expensive-run equivalents.

methods.name: designs
methods.doc:
``(design_low, design_high)``: a Sobol' design of ``n_low`` points, of which the first ``n_high`` are the
expensive ones. Nested on purpose -- the discrepancy is the difference between two values measured at the same
design, not between a value and an interpolation.

classes.name: MultiFidelityRun
classes.doc: The fitted models and the data behind them, with the two comparisons the workflow exists to make.

methods.name: gain
methods.doc: High-fidelity-only error divided by the co-kriging one, at the same number of expensive runs.

methods.name: verdict
methods.doc:
Whether the cheap level paid: decided on the equal-*count* gain, since the equal-*cost* one needs a declared
price. ``undecided`` when no oracle was given, which is the honest answer to a workflow run without truth.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: The co-kriging mean at ``design``, with the cheap level's own value there when ``use_low``.

methods.name: interval
methods.sig: (design, *, z: float = 1.96, use_low: bool = True) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
methods.doc:
``(mean, lower, upper)`` for :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.fidelity.serve`, whose tolerance is checked against
the band. The band is the co-kriging one, which
:meth:`~pinneapple_data.co_kriging.CoKriging.predict` documents as **approximate and erratic** (measured
1-sigma coverage 0.72): it is the right shape for a routing decision and not a guarantee.

methods.name: serves
methods.sig: (requests, solver: Callable, *, policy: FidelityPolicy | None = None, trust: Any = None, z: float = 1.96) -> FidelityReport
methods.doc: Answer ``requests`` with the co-kriging model, escalating to ``solver`` on the policy's terms (#161).

classes.name: MultiFidelityWorkflow
classes.sig: (low: Callable, high: Callable, bounds, *, plan: FidelityPlan | None = None, oracle: Callable | None = None, n_test: int = 120, test_seed: int = 0)
classes.doc:
The two levels as callables, the plan, and the run that fits both models.

>>> workflow = MultiFidelityWorkflow(low=coarse, high=fine, bounds=[(0.15, 0.85), (0.2, 2.0)],
...                                  plan=FidelityPlan(n_high=10, n_low=64, cost_ratio=0.02))
>>> run = workflow.run(oracle=exact)          # the oracle is optional; without it nothing is claimed
>>> print(run.table())

methods.name: test_designs
methods.doc: The ``(n_test, d)`` designs the errors are measured on: a Sobol' sequence of the same box.

methods.name: run
methods.doc: Evaluate the nested design, fit the co-kriging model and the high-fidelity-only one, score both.

functions.name: rod_fidelities
functions.sig: (low_cells: int = 8, high_cells: int = 32) -> tuple[Callable, Callable]
functions.doc:
The measured pair of solvers: the same 1-D Poisson problem at two ``fem`` mesh resolutions.

The problem comes from :func:`pinneapple_physics.active_design.source_rod` (a Gaussian source in a rod, with its
position and strength as the design variables) and the quantity of interest is the peak of the field. The cheap
level is the coarse mesh, the expensive one the fine mesh, and both are the *same physics* -- which is what makes
this a fidelity pair and not two functions that happen to be correlated.

Each level takes ``(n, d)`` designs and returns ``(n,)`` values, the contract every level here follows.

functions.name: benchmark_multifidelity_workflow
functions.sig: (*, repeats: int = 5, plan: FidelityPlan | None = None, low_cells: int = 8, high_cells: int = 32, truth_cells: int = 128, n_test: int = 120, extra_runs: Sequence[int] = (0, 1, 2, 3), seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
What the two levels buy, on a real solver pair, at an equal expensive count **and** at an equal cost.

Every repeat fits both models on the same data -- ``n_high`` expensive designs, ``n_low`` cheap ones, the expensive
ones nested inside the cheap ones -- and scores them on held-out designs against a solve far finer than the
expensive level. Then, for each number of extra expensive runs the 64 cheap ones could have bought instead, the
single-fidelity baseline is fitted on ``n_high + k`` expensive designs (the same box, its own Sobol' sequence) and
the two are compared. The comparison is put in **runs**, not in a price, because a run is what you can actually
buy: a ``cost_ratio`` of 0.01 and one of 0.02 both buy one more expensive run when the cheap budget is 64, and
reporting them as different prices would be a false precision.

Measured on this machine (``2026-11-25``), 5 repeats, ``plan = (n_high 10, n_low 64)``, 120 held-out designs,
``truth_cells = 128``:

===============================  =========================
quantity                          value
===============================  =========================
cheap model alone                 9.1e-2
high-fidelity only, 10 runs       1.8e-1
co-kriging, 10 + 64               7.8e-2
gain at equal expensive count     2.28 x (worst repeat 1.79 x)
gain at equal cost, 11 runs       1.36 x
gain at equal cost, 12 runs       0.74 x
break-even                        1 extra expensive run, i.e. cost_ratio 1/64 = 0.016
===============================  =========================

The ``0.74`` row is the honest half: **two** more expensive runs are worth more than all 64 cheap ones, so a coarse
model that is only three times cheaper than the fine one does not pay here, and the workflow says so. A benchmark
that compared equal *counts* only would have hidden it, which is why this one reports both.

children.summary: Two data levels in one workflow: the cheap model everywhere, the expensive solver where it pays (#35).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.numerics
pinneapple_analysis.numerics.convergence
children.doc:
Observed convergence orders and error curves, measured rather than assumed.

Every method in this package is described by the same two numbers: the order it converges at and the
error it reaches for a given effort. Both are *measured* here, from error values the caller already
has, so a test can assert that a scheme delivers the order its textbook formula promises -- and a user
can discover that it does not on their own problem.

The measurement
---------------
If the error of a discretisation decays like ``e(h) = C h^p`` then ``log e = log C + p log h``: ``p`` is
the slope of a straight line in log-log. :func:`fit_order` reports that slope with its standard error
and 95 % confidence interval, because a two-point estimate of an order is not an estimate at all -- it
is a coincidence that happens to have units of order.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_analysis.numerics.convergence import fit_order
    >>> h = np.array([0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125])
    >>> fit_order(h, 3.0 * h**2).order
    2.0000000000000004

The limitation, stated once for the whole module: a log-log slope is an *asymptotic* statement. It is
only the order of the scheme while the mesh is fine enough that the leading truncation term dominates
rounding and the higher-order terms. :meth:`OrderEstimate.agrees_with` is what a test should use, with
a tolerance, and the reported ``r_squared`` says how straight the line actually was.

The V-curve
-----------
Truncation error falls with ``h`` and round-off error grows like ``eps/h``, so the total error has a
minimum at some ``h_opt``. :func:`truncation_roundoff_balance` measures that curve and locates the
minimum instead of predicting it from a constant somebody guessed: the predicted and measured optimum
are compared, and a large ratio is itself a result worth reporting.

classes.name: OrderEstimate
classes.doc:
A measured convergence order with the uncertainty of the measurement.

``order`` is the exponent ``p`` in ``error ~ h**p``; ``ci95`` is the 95 % confidence interval of that
slope from the log-log least-squares fit; ``r_squared`` says how straight the log-log line was (1.0
is a perfect power law, which is what an asymptotic regime looks like).

methods.name: agrees_with
methods.doc: Whether the measured order is within ``rtol`` (relative) of ``expected``.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form for the numerical-lab page.

classes.name: ErrorCurve
classes.doc: An error measured at a sequence of step sizes (or costs), plus the order read off it.

methods.name: order
methods.doc: Fit ``error ~ C * step**p`` over the whole curve or its last ``tail`` (finest) points.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form: the raw curve plus its order -- what the lab page plots.

classes.name: VCurveResult
classes.doc:
The truncation/round-off trade-off, measured.

``optimal_step`` is the step at which the measured error is smallest, ``truncation_order`` the
measured order on the truncation-dominated branch (steps *above* the optimum, where the error grows
with ``h``), and ``roundoff_slope`` the measured exponent on the round-off-dominated branch (steps
below the optimum, negative because the error *grows* as the step shrinks, typically like
``eps/h`` -- slope -1 -- or ``eps/sqrt(h)`` -- slope -1/2).

methods.name: is_balanced
methods.doc: Whether the measured error actually has an interior minimum (both branches visible).

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form for the numerical-lab page.

functions.name: fit_order
functions.sig: (steps: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, errors: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, *, name: str = 'error') -> OrderEstimate
functions.doc:
Measure the convergence order ``p`` in ``error = C * step**p`` by log-log least squares.

Parameters
----------
steps : the step sizes (or mesh spacings, or cell counts -- anything that shrinks under refinement;
    for a cost axis the exponent means something else, so do not call it an order).
errors : the corresponding errors, positive and finite. At least two *distinct* steps are needed;
    with two points the slope is exact but has no computable uncertainty, and ``stderr`` is reported
    as NaN rather than zero -- a two-point fit is not evidence of a power law.

Raises
------
ValueError
    if fewer than two distinct, usable points remain. Returning an order from one point (or from a
    zero error) would be fabricating the number this function exists to measure.

functions.name: order_from_iterates
functions.sig: (iterates: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, limit: float, *, tail: int = 3) -> OrderEstimate
functions.doc:
Measure the convergence order of an iteration from its iterates.

For an iteration with error ``e_k = x_k - limit`` converging as ``e_{k+1} = C e_k^p`` with ``p > 1``,
three consecutive errors give ``p = log(e_{k+1}/e_k) / log(e_k/e_{k-1})``. The median of the last
``tail`` such estimates is returned, with the spread of those estimates as the standard error.

Only valid for ``p > 1``: for a linearly convergent iteration (bisection, fixed point) the same
formula divides two nearly equal quantities and returns noise, so the *contraction factor*
``e_{k+1}/e_k`` is the meaningful measurement -- see :func:`contraction_factors`. A ``limit`` equal to
the last iterate, or an iteration that never got below round-off, makes the errors constant and the
order meaningless; both produce NaN rather than a number.

functions.name: contraction_factors
functions.sig: (iterates: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, limit: float, *, tail: int = 3) -> tuple[float, ...]
functions.doc:
The last ``tail`` ratios ``|x_{k+1} - limit| / |x_k - limit|`` -- the measured factor of a linear iteration.

A bisection run gives ~0.5, a fixed-point iteration gives ~``|g'(x*)|``. This is the number that
matters for a linearly convergent method; the order is 1 by construction.

functions.name: richardson_extrapolate
functions.sig: (f_h: float, f_h2: float, order: float, *, r: float = 2.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Extrapolate two approximations at step ``h`` and ``h/r`` to ``h -> 0``.

With ``f(h) = f_exact + C h^p`` and ``f(h/r) = f_exact + C (h/r)^p``,
``f_exact = f(h/r) + (f(h/r) - f(h)) / (r^p - 1)``. Exactly the Roache formula used by
``pinneapple_analysis.verification.convergence``, kept here so the differentiation and quadrature
modules can extrapolate without depending on the verification package.

functions.name: truncation_roundoff_balance
functions.sig: (step_sizes: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, error_fn: Callable[[float], float], *, eps: float = float(np.finfo(float).eps), scale: float = 1.0, name: str = 'error') -> VCurveResult
functions.doc:
Evaluate ``error_fn(h)`` across a range of steps and locate the truncation/round-off minimum.

The total error of a finite-difference-like computation is ``C h^p + eps * S / h^q`` (``q = 1`` for a
first difference, ``q = 1/2`` for a centred one), so on a log-log plot it is a V: slope ``+p`` on the
left, ``-q`` on the right. Both slopes and the vertex are *measured* here.

``scale`` is the magnitude of the quantity being differentiated (``|f(x)|`` for a derivative): the
round-off term is relative to it, so the predicted optimum is
``h_opt = (q * eps * scale / (p * C))**(1/(p+q))`` with ``C`` taken from the measured truncation
branch. The ratio of predicted to measured ``h_opt`` is what says whether the classical balance
argument applies to this computation at all.

Raises ``ValueError`` if fewer than four usable steps are given: with fewer, neither branch can be fit
and any "optimum" would be the lowest of three arbitrary points.

children.summary: Observed convergence orders and error curves, measured rather than assumed.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.numerics.diagnostics
children.doc:
Why a numerical method failed, in a form an interface can show.

Every module of :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.numerics` that can fail returns a list of :class:`Diagnostic`
instead of only a flag: a stable ``code`` to key on, a severity, one sentence of *what happened*, one
of *why*, and one of *what to do*. The Studio page of the numerical lab and the Flow node render these
directly; a CLI prints :meth:`Diagnostic.format`.

    >>> from pinneapple_analysis.numerics.diagnostics import explain
    >>> d = explain("ODE.STIFF", ratio=1.2e6)
    >>> d.severity, d.code
    ('warning', 'ODE.STIFF')

The catalogue is data, not behaviour: a diagnostic never decides anything. The method that produced it
decides what to return; the diagnostic only says what a person reading the result needs to know. Adding
a code means adding one row to ``_CATALOGUE`` -- nothing else in the package changes.

classes.name: Diagnostic
classes.doc: One explanation of a numerical result: what happened, why, and what to do about it.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form (what the Studio page and the Flow node receive).

methods.name: format
methods.doc: One line for a CLI: ``[warning] ODE.STIFF: The problem is stiff -- use an implicit method``.

functions.name: explain
functions.sig: (code: str, **context) -> Diagnostic
functions.doc:
Look ``code`` up in the catalogue and attach the measured numbers as ``context``.

Raises ``KeyError`` for an unknown code: a diagnostic with no explanation would be a silent failure,
which is exactly what this module exists to avoid.

functions.name: catalogue
functions.sig: () -> tuple[str, ...]
functions.doc: Every code this package can emit, sorted -- the contract with the interface.

functions.name: has_code
functions.sig: (code: str) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether ``code`` is in the catalogue.

functions.name: worst
functions.sig: (diagnostics: list[Diagnostic] | tuple[Diagnostic, ...] | None) -> Diagnostic | None
functions.doc:
The most severe diagnostic of a list (error > warning > info), or ``None`` when there is none.

Result objects expose this as a convenience: an interface that shows one line shows this one.

children.summary: Why a numerical method failed, in a form an interface can show.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.numerics.floating_point
children.doc:
Floating point and error analysis: where digits go, and whether the problem or the code took them (#1056).

Five things a user of a numerical library needs to be able to see, each of them *measured* here rather
than quoted from a table:

1. **The dtype's own parameters** -- machine epsilon (by the classical halving loop), unit in the last
   place, the largest finite value and the smallest subnormal, measured for float16, float32 and
   float64.
2. **Catastrophic cancellation** -- the quadratic formula, ``log1p``/``expm1`` and the one-pass
   variance, each in its naive and its stable form, with the error against a reference computed in
   ``decimal`` at 60 digits.
3. **Compensated summation** -- naive, pairwise, Kahan and Neumaier, with the error *growth in n*
   measured (it is a slope on a log-log plot: ~1/2 for naive, ~1 for the worst case, ~0 for a
   compensated sum until it hits the floor).
4. **Conditioning against backward error** -- the verdict that matters: is the error the problem's fault
   (``cond`` large, ``forward ~ cond * backward``) or the algorithm's (``forward >> cond * backward``)?
5. **Interval arithmetic** for guaranteed bounds, and the precision floor of a residual evaluated in
   mixed precision (the reason a PINN's float32 loss stops improving).

The limitation, once: a condition number is a local, first-order statement about the *problem*. It says
nothing about the algorithm, and it does not apply away from the point where it was measured. Every
verdict here is therefore paired with the measured forward and backward errors that produced it --
a number, not a label.

classes.name: MachineParameters
classes.doc: The measured limits of one floating-point dtype.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form for the lab page.

classes.name: QuadraticRoots
classes.doc:
Both roots of ``a x^2 + b x + c = 0``, with the measured error of the formula that produced them.

``relative_errors`` is against the 50-digit ``decimal`` reference and is ``(nan, nan)`` when no
reference was requested. Roots are returned in decreasing magnitude.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form.

classes.name: VarianceComparison
classes.doc: The naive ``E[x^2] - E[x]^2`` against Welford's recurrence, both against an exact reference.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form.

classes.name: SummationGrowth
classes.doc:
How each summation's error grows with the number of terms, with the measured exponent.

``sizes`` are the sample counts, and each ``*_error`` array is the relative error at that size
against ``math.fsum``. ``growth_exponents`` fits ``error ~ n^q`` on the last half of the curve --
``q ~ 1/2`` for naive summation on random data (the random walk of roundings is the average case),
``q ~ 0`` for compensated or pairwise.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form for the lab page.

classes.name: ErrorBudget
classes.doc: Forward and backward error against the condition number -- the verdict, with its evidence.

methods.name: is_well_conditioned
methods.doc: Whether the condition number alone rules out rounding as the limiting factor.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form.

classes.name: Interval
classes.doc:
A closed interval with outward-rounded arithmetic -- a guaranteed enclosure.

Every operation computes the exact real result of the four endpoint combinations and then widens by
one ulp in each direction, so the returned interval provably contains the exact answer even though
the arithmetic underneath is rounded. That is the difference between an error *estimate* (which can
be wrong) and an error *bound* (which cannot, for the operations implemented here).

Limitation: with float64 endpoints and one-ulp outward rounding, the width of the result is the
accumulated rounding, which grows with the number of operations. An interval that is recomputed
through a long chain eventually says only "it is somewhere in here", which is still true but
useless -- interval arithmetic does not eliminate the conditioning of the problem, it makes the loss
visible.

methods.name: point
methods.doc: The degenerate interval ``[x, x]``.

methods.name: mid
methods.doc: Midpoint (not necessarily representable inside the interval after rounding; it is).

methods.name: width
methods.doc: Absolute width.

methods.name: relative_width
methods.doc: Width relative to the largest endpoint magnitude -- the number of digits still known.

methods.name: contains
methods.doc: Whether ``x`` lies in the interval.

methods.name: sqrt
methods.doc: Square root of an interval that must be non-negative: ``[sqrt(lo), sqrt(hi)]`` (monotone).

classes.name: PrecisionFloor
classes.doc: The residual floor a dtype imposes: the smallest residual a function can report there.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: JSON-able form.

functions.name: relative_error
functions.sig: (computed: float, reference: float) -> float
functions.doc:
``|computed - reference| / |reference|``, with a zero reference handled as an absolute error.

A relative error against zero is undefined; returning the absolute error there is the only honest
option, and it is what every comparison in this module uses.

functions.name: digits_lost
functions.sig: (computed: float, reference: float) -> float
functions.doc:
How many decimal digits the computation lost: ``-log10(relative_error)``.

``0`` means no digits lost (or better than the reference), ``8`` means the answer has 8 digits left
of the ~16 that float64 carries. Negative values mean the computation was *more* accurate than the
reference, which happens when the reference is the lower-precision one.

functions.name: machine_epsilon
functions.sig: (dtype: str | np.dtype = 'float64') -> float
functions.doc:
Measure machine epsilon: the smallest ``eps`` with ``1 + eps != 1`` in ``dtype``.

The halving loop is the definition, run in the dtype itself: start from 1 and keep halving while
``1 + eps`` still rounds up to something larger than 1. It halts because once ``eps`` is below half
an ulp of 1 the sum rounds back to 1. Returns ``2**-52`` for float64, ``2**-23`` for float32 and
``2**-10`` for float16.

functions.name: ulp
functions.sig: (x: float, dtype: str | np.dtype = 'float64') -> float
functions.doc:
The unit in the last place at ``x``: the distance to the next representable number.

Equals ``eps * 2**floor(log2|x|)`` in the normal range, which is why a condition number multiplies
the error of a *relative* perturbation by the magnitude of the quantity, not by eps alone.

functions.name: machine_parameters
functions.sig: (dtype: str | np.dtype = 'float64') -> MachineParameters
functions.doc:
Measure the limits of ``dtype``: epsilon by halving, the subnormal floor by halving to zero.

Epsilon and the smallest subnormal are measured, because both are the answer to a loop a user can
read. The largest finite value is taken from ``np.finfo``: doubling up to it would need 2**24 steps
in float32, which measures nothing that the table does not already guarantee. ``float16`` is included because a neural network's forward pass
routinely runs there, and its epsilon is nine decimal digits coarser than float64's.

functions.name: quadratic_roots_reference
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, c: float, *, digits: int = 50) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc:
The two real roots computed in ``decimal`` at ``digits`` significant digits -- the reference.

``decimal`` is in the standard library, so this module measures cancellation without a dependency.
Raises ``ValueError`` when the discriminant is negative (complex roots are out of scope here, and
returning a NaN would hide the caller's mistake).

functions.name: quadratic_roots
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, c: float, *, method: str = 'stable', reference: bool = True) -> QuadraticRoots
functions.doc:
Roots of the quadratic, by the naive or the cancellation-free formula.

The naive formula ``(-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a)`` loses every digit of the root that subtracts
two nearly equal numbers -- which is the *small* root whenever ``b^2 >> 4ac``. The stable form
computes ``q = -(b + sign(b) sqrt(disc)) / 2`` first, then uses ``r1 = q/a`` and ``r2 = c/q``:
Vieta's identity ``r1 r2 = c/a`` supplies the second root by multiplication instead of subtraction.

Example where the naive formula is worthless: ``x^2 - 1e8 x + 1 = 0`` -- the small root is 1e-8, and
``-b + sqrt(b^2-4ac)`` cancels all of its leading digits.

Parameters
----------
method : ``"stable"`` (default) or ``"naive"``, for comparing the two.

Raises ``ValueError`` for a negative discriminant or ``a == 0``.

functions.name: log1p_expm1_comparison
functions.sig: (x: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Measure what ``log(1+x)`` and ``exp(x)-1`` lose against ``log1p``/``expm1`` near zero.

``log(1+x)`` first rounds ``1+x`` to the dtype, so for ``|x| < eps`` the addition throws the whole
information away; ``exp(x)-1`` subtracts two numbers that both round to 1. Returns absolute errors
for the naive and the stable form, both against the standard library's correctly rounded
``math.log1p``/``math.expm1``.

The stable forms are not "better approximations" -- they are the same function computed without the
intermediate that rounds.

functions.name: variance_naive
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
``mean(x^2) - mean(x)^2`` -- the textbook shortcut, and the wrong one for large means.

The two means are each of size ``mean^2``, and their difference is the variance. When the variance
is small compared with the mean, the subtraction cancels all the significant digits of both terms:
the result carries the rounding error of the *large* quantities.

functions.name: variance_welford
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
Welford's one-pass recurrence: no subtraction of two large, nearly equal means.

``x -> x + (v - x)/n`` then ``M2 -> M2 + (v - x_new)(v - x_old)``. The second factor is the
*residual* of each sample, so the accumulated quantity is of the size of the variance throughout.
Returns the population variance (divide by ``n``), to match :func:`variance_naive`.

functions.name: variance_comparison
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> VarianceComparison
functions.doc:
Both one-pass variances against ``math.fsum``-based exact arithmetic.

The reference subtracts the exact mean (a correctly rounded ``fsum`` quotient) from each sample and
sums the squares with ``fsum``, so it carries no cancellation of its own.

functions.name: naive_sum
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
Left-to-right accumulation. Its error grows like ``n * eps * sum|x|``: the running total is
rounded once per term, and each rounding is amplified by the size the total later reaches.

functions.name: kahan_sum
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
Kahan compensated summation: keep the lost low-order bits in a compensation term.

``y = v - c`` ; ``t = s + y`` ; ``c = (t - s) - y``. The compensation is subtracted from the next
term, so the error no longer grows with ``n`` in the usual regime (its worst-case bound is
``2 eps sum|x|``, independent of ``n``). It assumes the compiler does not reassociate, which is true
for CPython floats.

functions.name: neumaier_sum
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
Neumaier's variant of Kahan: also correct when a term is larger than the running total.

Plain Kahan fails when ``|v| > |s|``, because the compensation ``(t - s) - y`` then evaluates to
zero. Neumaier branches on the magnitudes and adds the compensation at the end, which makes the
result as accurate as a doubly compensated sum for a wider range of inputs.

functions.name: pairwise_sum
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
Recursive bisection: ``O(log n)`` error growth instead of ``O(n)``, at no extra rounding cost.

Each partial sum is short, so few roundings accumulate; the depth is ``log2 n`` and the error bound
is ``eps log2(n) sum|x|``, which for a million terms is 20 roundings rather than a million.

functions.name: summation_error_growth
functions.sig: (sizes: Sequence[int] = (10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000), *, seed: int = 0) -> SummationGrowth
functions.doc:
Measure the relative error of each summation method against ``fsum`` as ``n`` grows.

The sample is uniform in ``[0, 1]``, so the partial sums grow like ``n`` and the *relative* error
isolates the number of roundings instead of being confounded by the growth of the sum. The naive
roundings add up like a random walk, which is why its exponent is about ``1/2`` and not ``1`` (``1``
is the worst case, reached by data with one huge term and many tiny ones). ``fsum`` is exactly
rounded, so it is a reference and not a competitor.

A compensated method can report exactly zero error at these sizes; its exponent is then NaN, which
means "at the floor of this measurement" and not "unknown".

The exponent is fit on the upper half of the size range, where the asymptotic regime holds.

functions.name: error_budget
functions.sig: (condition_number: float, forward_error_rel: float, backward_error_rel: float, *, tolerance: float = 10.0) -> ErrorBudget
functions.doc:
Decide whether an observed error is the problem's fault or the algorithm's.

The first-order model is ``forward_error ~ cond * backward_error``: a backward-stable algorithm
turns a perturbation of the input into at most a ``cond``-fold perturbation of the output. So:

* ``forward <= tolerance * cond * backward`` -> the algorithm is doing its job; if the error is
  large it is because the *problem* amplifies. Verdict ``"problem"``.
* ``forward > tolerance * cond * backward`` -> the algorithm amplifies more than the conditioning
  requires. Verdict ``"algorithm"``.
* ``cond < 10`` -> verdict ``"well-conditioned"`` regardless, because the amplification is bounded
  by a small number and neither label is informative.

``tolerance`` is the factor by which the model may be off before the verdict flips (10 is generous
on purpose: the model is first-order and the errors are measured).

The verdict names what to change, which is the only actionable content: a bad condition number is
fixed by reformulating the problem, a bad algorithm by replacing it.

functions.name: measured_condition_number
functions.sig: (function: Callable[[float], float], x: float, *, relative_step: float = 1e-07) -> float
functions.doc:
Measure ``cond = |df/f| / |dx/x|`` at ``x`` with a forward perturbation.

This is the empirical definition, not a symbolic derivative: perturb the input by
``relative_step``, evaluate, and take the ratio of relative changes. It is one-sided, so for a
function with a large second derivative use a small step (``relative_step ~ 1e-7`` in float64) --
too small and the difference of two function values cancels, too large and the curvature moves the
answer. Both limits are the same V-curve this package measures elsewhere.

functions.name: interval_quadratic_roots
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, c: float) -> tuple[Interval, Interval]
functions.doc:
Enclose both real roots of the quadratic using interval arithmetic on the *naive* formula.

The point of doing it on the naive formula is that the enclosure for the small root comes out wide
-- not because the arithmetic is wrong, but because the formula genuinely cannot determine that root
to more than a few digits in double precision. The wide interval is the honest answer, and it is
