functions.doc:
Run the model on ``n`` samples with all inputs varying, and on the same samples with ``frozen`` inputs held at
their nominal value (the median, or ``at[name]``). Returns per output the variance ratio (frozen / full) and
the largest and 95th-percentile pointwise change relative to the output's standard deviation.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.morris
children.doc:
Morris elementary effects: a cheap screening of which inputs matter, ``r (d + 1)`` evaluations.

Each of ``r`` trajectories starts at a random point of a ``levels``-level grid of the unit hypercube and moves one
input at a time by ``delta = levels / (2 (levels - 1))``, in random order (Morris 1991, Technometrics 33:161). The
elementary effect of input ``i`` is the output change per unit of its *normalised* range (the unit hypercube, mapped
to each distribution through its inverse CDF; for an unbounded distribution the unit interval covers the
0.5 %-99.5 % quantiles). Per input: ``mu`` (mean effect), ``mu_star`` (mean absolute effect, Campolongo et al. 2007:
the importance measure) and ``sigma`` (spread: nonlinearity or interactions), with a bootstrap interval on
``mu_star`` over trajectories.

functions.name: morris_design
functions.sig: (d: int, r: int = 20, levels: int = 4, seed: int = 0) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Unit-hypercube trajectories ``(r (d + 1), d)``, the input moved at each step ``(r, d)`` and its sign.

functions.sig: (fn, space, r: int = 20, levels: int = 4, seed: int = 0, n_boot: int = 500, level: float = 0.95, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> MorrisResult
functions.doc: Morris screening of ``fn`` over ``space`` with ``r`` trajectories (cost ``r (d + 1)`` evaluations).

children.summary: Morris elementary effects: a cheap screening of which inputs matter, r (d + 1) evaluations.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.sobol
children.doc:
Variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity indices with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Design: two independent quasi-random matrices ``A`` and ``B`` (a scrambled Sobol sequence in ``2 d`` dimensions,
mapped to each input's distribution through its inverse CDF) and the matrices ``AB_i`` (``A`` with column ``i`` from
``B``); for second-order indices also ``BA_i``. Estimators:

- first order ``S_i``: Saltelli et al. (2010), Comput. Phys. Commun. 181:259, eq. (b) of table 2,
  ``mean(f(B) (f(AB_i) - f(A))) / V``;
- total ``ST_i``: Jansen (1999), ``mean((f(A) - f(AB_i))^2) / (2 V)``;
- second order ``S_ij``: Saltelli (2002), Comput. Phys. Commun. 145:280,
  ``mean(f(BA_i) f(AB_j) - f(A) f(B)) / V - S_i - S_j``;

with ``V`` the variance of ``[f(A), f(B)]``. Confidence intervals: percentile bootstrap over the rows of the design
(Archer et al. 1997). Cost: ``N (d + 2)`` model evaluations, ``N (2 d + 2)`` with second order.

:func:`first_order_given_data` estimates first-order indices from an existing sample (a dataset, a campaign's runs)
without a designed experiment, by the correlation-ratio estimator on equal-count bins.

classes.name: SobolIndices
classes.doc:
Sobol indices per output (rows) and input (columns), with ``level`` bootstrap intervals ``*_ci`` of shape
``(2, m, d)`` (lower, upper). ``S2`` is ``(m, d, d)`` when second order was requested.

methods.name: interaction
methods.doc: ``ST - S1``: the share of variance from interactions of each input with the others.

methods.name: ranking
methods.doc: Inputs by decreasing total index for one output.

fields: method: str = 'Saltelli (2010) first order, Jansen (1999) total, Saltelli (2002) second order'

functions.doc:
Inputs ``X`` to evaluate, stacked as ``[A; B; AB_1..AB_d; (BA_1..BA_d)]``, and the layout to read them back.
``n`` is rounded up to a power of two (the balance property of the Sobol sequence).

functions.doc:
First-order and total Sobol indices (and optionally second order) of ``fn`` over ``space``.

Parameters
----------
fn : model evaluated on an ``(n, d)`` array, returning ``(n,)`` or ``(n, m)``.
space : uncertain inputs (see :func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.distributions.as_space`).
n : base sample size ``N`` (rounded up to a power of two); cost ``N (d + 2)`` evaluations.
n_boot, level : bootstrap resamples and confidence level of the intervals.

functions.name: first_order_given_data
functions.sig: (X, y, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, n_bins: int | None = None, n_boot: int = 200, level: float = 0.95, seed: int = 0) -> dict
functions.doc:
First-order indices from an existing sample ``(X, y)`` with independent inputs: ``Var(E[y | x_i]) / Var(y)``
estimated on ``n_bins`` equal-count bins of each input (default ``sqrt(n)``, at most 50), with the bias of the bin
means (within-bin variance / bin size) subtracted. Interactions and totals need a designed experiment
(:func:`sobol_indices`); correlated inputs make these indices hard to interpret.

functions.name: sobol_from_runs
functions.sig: (space, n: int, run_ids, Y, second_order: bool = False, seed: int = 0, n_boot: int = 200, level: float = 0.95, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> SobolIndices

Indices from runs of the design ``saltelli_design(space, n, second_order, seed)`` done elsewhere (OpenFOAM,
CalculiX, a campaign runner): ``run_ids`` are the row numbers of the design (any order), ``Y`` their outputs.
Every run of the design is needed; a missing or failed run raises ``ValueError`` naming it.

children.summary: Variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity indices with bootstrap confidence intervals.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.study
children.doc:
One sensitivity study: which parameters really control each response, and which can be frozen.

:func:`sensitivity_study` runs, on one model and one parameter space: Morris screening, Sobol first/total (and
optionally second-order) indices with bootstrap intervals, main-effect and ICE curves, local derivatives at the
nominal point (autodiff when the model has a torch function), the freeze recommendation and its direct check.
:func:`study_cost` gives the number of model evaluations before anything runs.

When ``paths_fn`` is given the model is a surrogate whose own error is to be propagated (#927): the indices are then
those of the mean path, their intervals are the combined ones of
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.surrogate_error.sobol_from_paths` (so the freeze rule uses the combined upper
bound), ``sobol.sources`` says what the interval includes, and ``ranking_stability`` reports how the ranking moves
across the draws.

functions.name: study_cost
functions.sig: (d: int, n_sobol: int = 1024, second_order: bool = False, r_morris: int = 20, n_grid: int = 15, n_background: int = 64, n_verify: int = 512, morris_on: bool = True, effects_on: bool = True) -> dict
functions.doc: Model evaluations of each part of :func:`sensitivity_study` (``n_sobol`` rounded up to a power of two).

functions.name: sensitivity_study
functions.sig: (model, space, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, n_sobol: int = 1024, second_order: bool = False, r_morris: int = 20, n_grid: int = 15, n_background: int = 64, threshold: float = 0.01, n_boot: int = 200, level: float = 0.95, n_verify: int = 512, nominal: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, fixed: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, morris_on: bool = True, effects_on: bool = True, exact: Ma...
functions.doc:
Run the study.

``model`` is a :class:`pinneapple_analysis.study_models.StudyModel`; ``space`` lists the varied parameters
(distributions); model inputs not in ``space`` are held at ``fixed[name]``. ``outputs`` selects responses
(default all). ``exact`` (``{"S1": [...], "ST": [...]}`` for the first output) adds the error of the estimate
against known indices (benchmark functions).

``paths_fn`` makes the study honest about a surrogate: it receives the ``(n_design, d)`` design in the varied
parameters (the same array ``model.predict`` is called with, mapped through the fixed inputs) and returns
``(n_paths, n_design, len(outputs))`` — posterior paths from
:func:`~pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.surrogate_error.gp_posterior_paths`, one row per ensemble member, or
residual-perturbed outputs. The reported intervals then cover the surrogate's error as well as the sampling.

children.summary: One sensitivity study: which parameters really control each response, and which can be frozen.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.surrogate_error
children.doc:
The surrogate's own error inside the Sobol intervals, and the stability of the ranking (#927).

:func:`sobol_indices` reports percentile-bootstrap intervals over the Saltelli sample. Those cover the Monte Carlo
error of the indices *for the model as given*; they do not cover the model's prediction error, so a surrogate with a
few dozen training points gets the same narrow intervals as the solver it stands for. This module propagates that
second source:

- :func:`gp_posterior_paths`: posterior sample paths of a fitted Gaussian process, the ``N_s`` realisations of
  Marrel, Iooss, Laurent & Roustant (2009), *Calculations of Sobol indices for the Gaussian process metamodel*,
  Reliab. Eng. Syst. Saf. 94(3):742. Computing the indices on every path gives a distribution instead of one number;
- :func:`ensemble_paths`: one path per member of an ensemble (MLP ensemble, deep ensemble, a zoo model with members);
- :func:`paths_from_residuals`: outputs perturbed with resampled calibration residuals (signed residuals of the
  Surrogate Studio / Uncertainty Lab). This one is weaker by construction: it ignores the residuals' correlation
  structure, and the docstring says so.

:func:`sobol_from_paths` (and its convenience wrapper :func:`sobol_with_paths`) turns those paths into

- a **combined interval**, from a nested bootstrap that resamples both the path and the rows of the design, reported
  in the usual ``S1_ci``/``ST_ci`` so that everything downstream (the freeze rule included) uses it;
- the **decomposition**: the width from Monte Carlo sampling alone (the old interval), from the surrogate alone, and
  the variance share of each;
- the **ranking stability**: per input the probability that its rank is unchanged and that it is in the top *k*,
  and the Kendall tau (1938) between each draw and the reported ranking.

The measurement that backs this is in ``tests/test_sensitivity_surrogate_error.py``: on Ishigami fitted with a GP on
30, 100 and 300 points, the coverage of the combined interval against the exact indices is counted, next to the
coverage of the bootstrap-only interval, which under-covers for the poor surrogate.

classes.name: SurrogateError
classes.doc:
Where the width of the reported interval comes from, and how stable the ranking is.

``bootstrap_only``, ``surrogate_only`` and ``combined`` each hold ``S1_ci``/``ST_ci`` of shape ``(2, m, d)``
like :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.sobol.SobolIndices`. ``variance_share`` splits the variance of the
index over the combined draws into the part that the row resampling explains and the part the path draws
explain; ``dominates`` says the surrogate part is the larger one.

methods.name: table
methods.doc: Per input, in the reported order: the two intervals side by side and the ranking stability.

functions.name: gp_posterior_paths
functions.sig: (gp, X, n_paths: int = 100, seed: int = 0, jitter: float = 1e-09, subtract_noise: bool = False) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``n_paths`` draws of a fitted Gaussian process at ``X``, conditioned on its training data.

``gp`` is a fitted ``sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor`` (one output) or a sequence of them (one
per output). Each draw is a function, so the indices computed on it see the surrogate's error as a whole, with
the spatial correlation the GP believes in — unlike perturbing the output point by point.

``subtract_noise`` removes the fitted white-noise variance from the diagonal of the posterior covariance, giving
paths of the *latent* function rather than of a noisy observation of it (the default matches what
``gp.predict(return_std=True)`` reports).

functions.name: ensemble_paths
functions.sig: (members, X, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
One path per ensemble member: ``members`` are callables ``X -> (n,) or (n, m)`` (the members of an ensemble,
a zoo model's members). Indices on each path are the indices of that member; the spread across paths is the
ensemble spread, moved from the output to the indices.

functions.name: paths_from_residuals
functions.sig: (pred, residuals, n_paths: int = 100, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``pred`` plus resampled calibration residuals, ``n_paths`` times.

Use the **signed** residuals ``y - pred`` of the calibration split (``conformal_scores`` gives absolute scores;
take the sign from the calibration set). Each draw resamples the residuals independently at every design point,
which is the weak part: the surrogate's error is spatially correlated, and this ignores it. It over-states the
variance of the indices when the errors are smooth and under-states it when they are biased in blocks.

functions.name: ranking_stability
functions.sig: (ST_draws, names: Sequence[str], top_k: Sequence[int] = (1, 2, 3), reference: np.ndarray | None = None, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
How stable a ranking by total index is across draws.

``ST_draws`` is ``(n_draws, m, d)`` (one total-index vector per draw). For each output it reports, per input:
``rank_stability`` (the fraction of draws where its rank is the reference rank), ``p_top_k`` per ``k``,
``rank_median`` and the 5-95 % band of its rank; and per output the Kendall tau of every draw against the
reference ranking. The reference is the ranking of the median total index (or of ``reference`` when given).

functions.name: sobol_from_paths
functions.sig: (paths, layout: dict, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None, level: float = 0.95, n_draws: int = 200, top_k: Sequence[int] = (1, 2, 3), seed: int = 0, method: str = '', sources: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> SobolIndices
functions.doc:
Sobol indices of a design whose outputs are not one number but a set of ``paths``.

``paths`` is ``(n_paths, n_design)`` or ``(n_paths, n_design, m)`` on the design of
:func:`~pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.sobol.saltelli_design` (the ``layout`` it returns). The reported
``S1``/``ST`` come from the mean over the paths (the surrogate's point prediction); their ``*_ci`` are the
**combined** interval, resampling the path and the rows of the design together. ``result.surrogate_error`` holds
the decomposition and the ranking stability, and ``result.to_dict()["sources"]`` says what the interval includes.

functions.name: sobol_with_paths
functions.sig: (paths_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], space, n: int = 1024, second_order: bool = False, level: float = 0.95, n_draws: int = 200, seed: int = 0, outputs: Sequence[str] | None = None, top_k: Sequence[int] = (1, 2, 3), method: str = '', sources: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> SobolIndices
functions.doc:
:func:`sobol_from_paths` on the design of ``saltelli_design(space, n, second_order, seed)``:
``paths_fn`` receives the ``(n_design, d)`` inputs and returns ``(n_paths, n_design[, m])``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.testfunctions
children.doc:
Benchmark functions with closed-form Sobol indices, to check a sensitivity estimator against the exact answer.

- Ishigami & Homma (1990): ``f = sin x1 + a sin^2 x2 + b x3^4 sin x1`` on ``[-pi, pi]^3``; indices from Sobol &
  Levitan (1999), also tabulated in Saltelli et al. (2008), *Global Sensitivity Analysis: The Primer*, sec. 4.9.
- Sobol' G function: ``f = prod (|4 x_i - 2| + a_i) / (1 + a_i)`` on ``[0, 1]^d``; partial variances
  ``V_i = 1 / (3 (1 + a_i)^2)`` (Saltelli & Sobol' 1995).

children.doc:
Global and local sensitivity analysis: which parameters really control the result.

=========================================  =====================================================================
``sobol_indices(fn, space, n)``            first-order, total (and second-order) Sobol indices, bootstrap intervals
``saltelli_design`` / ``sobol_from_runs``  the same from runs done elsewhere (OpenFOAM, CalculiX, a campaign)
``first_order_given_data(X, y)``           first-order indices from an existing dataset (no designed experiment)
``morris(fn, space, r)``                   elementary-effects screening (mu*, sigma), ``r (d + 1)`` evaluations
``effect_curves(fn, space)``               main effects (partial dependence) and ICE curves
``local_derivatives(fn, x0, torch_fn=)``   Jacobian by autodiff (torch) or central differences
``freeze_recommendation`` / ``verify_freeze``  which inputs can be fixed, and the direct check of that claim
``testfunctions``                          Ishigami and Sobol' G with their exact indices
``sensitivity_study`` / ``study_cost``     all of the above on one model, and its cost in evaluations
``gp_posterior_paths`` / ``ensemble_paths``  surrogate-error sources: GP posterior paths, one path per ensemble member
``paths_from_residuals``                   the same from calibration residuals (the weak source: no correlation)
``sobol_from_paths`` / ``sobol_with_paths``  Sobol indices whose intervals also cover the surrogate's error
``ranking_stability``                      rank-unchanged and top-k probabilities, Kendall tau across the draws
=========================================  =====================================================================

Inputs are described as in :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.distributions` (uniform, normal, truncated normal,
lognormal, triangular). The estimators are checked against the exact indices of the Ishigami and G functions in
``tests/test_sensitivity.py``; the coverage of the intervals that include the surrogate's error is counted in
``tests/test_sensitivity_surrogate_error.py``. The older
:class:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.GlobalSensitivity` (uniform bounds, no intervals) remains for its
callers.
children.summary: Global and local sensitivity analysis: which parameters really control the result.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation
pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.estimator
children.doc:
``StateEstimator``: sensors → state → physics → prediction → correction, behind one name (#215).

The four filters existed (or now exist) as separate classes with the same recursion. This puts the choice behind one
object, so a twin can say which filter it uses and a case can change it without being rewritten:

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.estimator import StateEstimator
    >>> model = {"n_state": 2, "n_obs": 1, "f": lambda x: x, "h": lambda x: x[:1]}
    >>> est = StateEstimator("ukf", **model).initialize(np.zeros(2), np.eye(2))
    >>> report = est.run(np.zeros((5, 1)), truth=np.zeros((5, 2)))    # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> report.rmse                                                   # doctest: +SKIP
    array([0., 0.])

What the report carries is the point: the filtered states, the innovations, and — when the truth is known, as it is
in a twin case and never in the field — the error per component. A filter that is not compared with the truth it is
supposed to recover has not been shown to work.

classes.name: EstimateReport
classes.doc: What a filtered time series came to: the states, the innovations, and the error against the truth.

classes.name: StateEstimator
classes.sig: (method: str = 'ekf', *, n_state: int, n_obs: int, f, h, Q: np.ndarray | None = None, R: np.ndarray | None = None, seed: int = 0, **options) -> None
classes.doc:
One filter, chosen by name, driven over a stream of observations.

Parameters
----------
method:
    ``"ekf"`` (linearised, finite-difference or analytic Jacobians), ``"ukf"`` (sigma points, no Jacobian),
    ``"enkf"`` (ensemble, for high dimension) or ``"particle"`` (a full non-Gaussian belief).
n_state, n_obs:
    Dimensions of the state and the observation.
f, h:
    State transition and observation operator.
Q, R:
    Process and observation noise covariances.
options:
    Handed to the chosen filter: ``n_ens``/``inflation`` (EnKF), ``alpha``/``beta``/``kappa`` (UKF),
    ``n_particles``/``ess_fraction`` (particle).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman
children.doc:
Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) for
sequential state estimation / data assimilation.

Relocated from ``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py``
(a single-file implementation tightly coupled *by location*, not by
API, to ``DigitalTwin``) so it can be used standalone -- fuse a plain
physics model with a stream of sensor observations -- without building
a full ``DigitalTwin``. The implementation already operated purely on
plain ``np.ndarray`` state/observation vectors and user-supplied
transition/observation callables ``f``/``h``; it never referenced
``DigitalTwin``, ``SystemState``, or ``Observation``, so no API
generalization was needed for the move -- this is the same code,
verbatim, at a general-purpose home.

``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py`` now contains
a thin re-export shim pointing back here (the same convention as
``pinneapple_models/registry.py``), so every existing caller
(``DigitalTwin._build_default_filter`` included) keeps working
unchanged.

This is classic sequential/recursive *state* filtering (predict ->
observe -> update, repeated over a time series) -- not to be confused
with ``pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ensemble_kalman``'s
``EnsembleKalmanInversion`` / ``IteratedEKI`` (EKI/TEKI), which are
derivative-free *parameter* estimation methods that iterate an
ensemble to a converged parameter estimate rather than filtering a
state through time.

References
----------
- Evensen (2009) "Data Assimilation: The Ensemble Kalman Filter"
- Asch, Bocquet, Nodet (2016) "Data Assimilation"

classes.doc:
Extended Kalman Filter for state estimation.

State: x ∈ R^n
Observation: y ∈ R^m

Dynamics:   x_k = f(x_{k-1}) + w_k,  w ~ N(0, Q)
Observation: y_k = h(x_k)    + v_k,  v ~ N(0, R)

Parameters
----------
n_state : int        state dimension
n_obs : int          observation dimension
f : callable         state transition x_{k-1} -> x_k
h : callable         observation function x_k -> y_k
Q : np.ndarray       process noise covariance (n_state, n_state)
R : np.ndarray       observation noise covariance (n_obs, n_obs)
F_jac : callable     Jacobian of f wrt x (optional; uses finite diff if None)
H_jac : callable     Jacobian of h wrt x (optional; uses finite diff if None)

``d`` = distance / half-width (zero for d >= 2).

functions.sig: (ens: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, hx: np.ndarray, r_var: np.ndarray, *, loc_xy: np.ndarray | None = None, loc_yy: np.ndarray | None = None, inflation: float = 1.0, rng: np.random.Generator | None = None) -> np.ndarray

Stochastic EnKF analysis (perturbed observations; Burgers et al. 1998, Mon. Wea. Rev. 126:1719) of an
ensemble ``ens`` (N, n_state) given observations ``y`` (m,), their forecast equivalents ``hx`` (N, m) and
independent observation-error variances ``r_var`` (m,).

``loc_xy`` (n_state, m) and ``loc_yy`` (m, m) are Schur-product localisation weights (e.g. :func:`gaspari_cohn`
of distances); ``inflation`` multiplies the forecast anomalies first. Returns the analysis ensemble (N,
n_state). Use it with any batched model: forecast the N members, call this, repeat.

children.summary: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) for sequential state estimation / data assimilation.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.unscented
children.doc:
Unscented Kalman filter and particle filter: the two the module was missing (#215).

The EKF linearises ``f`` and ``h`` with a Jacobian and is wrong wherever the nonlinearity bends inside the step; the
EnKF samples the covariance with an ensemble and needs a large one to be stable. The UKF carries the covariance
through a small, deterministic set of sigma points — no Jacobian, no sampling noise — and the particle filter keeps a
full non-Gaussian belief, which is the only one of the four that can represent two modes.

All of them drive the same ``f``/``h`` callables and the same ``predict`` → ``update`` → ``step`` recursion as
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman`, so a case can change filter without being rewritten.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.unscented import UnscentedKalmanFilter
    >>> ukf = UnscentedKalmanFilter(2, 1, f=lambda x: x, h=lambda x: x[:1], Q=1e-4 * np.eye(2), R=0.01 * np.eye(1))
    >>> ukf.initialize(np.array([0.0, 1.0]), np.eye(2))
    >>> out = ukf.step(np.array([0.6]))          # doctest: +SKIP

classes.name: UnscentedKalmanFilter
classes.sig: (n_state: int, n_obs: int, f, h, Q: np.ndarray | None = None, R: np.ndarray | None = None, *, alpha: float = 0.001, beta: float = 2.0, kappa: float | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Unscented Kalman filter: sigma points carry mean and covariance through ``f`` and ``h``.

Parameters
----------
n_state, n_obs:
    Dimensions of the state and of the observation.
f, h:
    State transition ``x_{k-1} -> x_k`` and observation operator ``x_k -> y_k``. Neither needs a Jacobian.
Q, R:
    Process and observation noise covariances.
alpha, beta, kappa:
    Spread of the sigma points (``alpha``), how much the prior is trusted for the covariance of the propagated
    mean (``beta``), and the secondary scaling (``kappa``, ``3 - n`` by default). The defaults are the ones in
    Julier and Uhlmann (1997) and Wan and van der Merwe (2000); ``alpha = 1`` is the plain unscented transform.

methods.name: sigma_points
methods.doc: ``(2n + 1, n)``: the mean and the symmetric columns of ``sqrt((n + lambda) P)`` around it.

methods.name: initialize
methods.sig: (x0: np.ndarray, P0: np.ndarray | None = None) -> None

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: Propagate every sigma point through ``f``; the covariance it comes back with is the unscented one.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Fuse observation ``y``: the gain comes from the cross-covariance of state and observation.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Predict + update in one call, like the EKF and the EnKF.

classes.name: ParticleFilter
classes.sig: (n_state: int, n_obs: int, f, h, Q: np.ndarray | None = None, R: np.ndarray | None = None, *, n_particles: int = 2000, ess_fraction: float = 0.5, seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Bootstrap (sequential importance resampling) particle filter.

The belief is the cloud itself, so it can be two modes wide — which none of the Kalman family can — at the cost
of needing enough particles for the tail and a model whose noise can be sampled.

Parameters
----------
n_particles:
    Size of the cloud. Doubling it halves the Monte Carlo error of a mean in the usual square-root way.
f, h:
    State transition and observation operator, as in the other filters.
Q, R:
    Process and observation noise covariances; both are used as Gaussian proposals.
ess_fraction:
    Resample when the effective sample size falls below this fraction of the cloud. Resampling every step throws
    away information; never resampling lets a handful of particles carry the whole belief.

methods.name: ess
methods.doc: Effective sample size: how many particles the weights are really worth (1 / sum w^2).

methods.name: initialize
methods.sig: (x0: np.ndarray, P0: np.ndarray | None = None) -> None

methods.name: initialize_from_samples
methods.doc:
Start from a cloud somebody else drew — the case a Gaussian cannot start from: two modes, a bound, a
previous run. ``samples`` is ``(n_state, n_particles)``.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Reweight by the Gaussian likelihood of ``y`` under each particle, then resample if the cloud collapsed.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Predict + update in one call.

children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation -- Sequential state estimation
(data assimilation) building blocks.

Relocated from ``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py``
(implementation code coupled to ``DigitalTwin`` only by its location in
the tree, not by its API) so any use case -- ``examples/``, other
``pinneapple_*`` packages, or standalone scripts -- can fuse a plain
physics model with streaming/batch sensor observations directly,
without building a full ``DigitalTwin``.
``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py`` now contains
a thin re-export shim pointing back here (the same convention as
``pinneapple_models/registry.py``), so every existing caller keeps
working unchanged.

Sub-modules
-----------
kalman
    ``ExtendedKalmanFilter`` (linearized EKF, finite-difference or
    user-supplied Jacobians) and ``EnsembleKalmanFilter`` (stochastic
    EnKF for higher-dimensional / non-linear systems). Both drive a
    user-supplied state-transition ``f`` and observation operator ``h``
    through the classic predict -> observe -> update recursion over a
    time series of plain ``np.ndarray`` states and observations.
unscented
    ``UnscentedKalmanFilter`` (sigma points: no Jacobian and no sampling
    noise) and ``ParticleFilter`` (a full non-Gaussian belief, the only one
    that can be two modes wide).
estimator
    ``StateEstimator`` behind one name: pick the filter by ``"ekf"``,
    ``"ukf"``, ``"enkf"`` or ``"particle"``, run the stream, and get the
    states, the innovations and — when a truth is given — the error.

Note
----
This is sequential/recursive *state* filtering, not to be confused
with ``pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ensemble_kalman``'s
``EnsembleKalmanInversion`` / ``IteratedEKI`` (Ensemble Kalman
**Inversion**), a derivative-free *parameter* estimation technique that
iterates an ensemble to a converged parameter estimate rather than
filtering a state through time.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate
pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.benchmark_workflow
children.doc:
The standard model-benchmarking workflow (#1191): candidates on one protocol, ranked with intervals, a winner
named only when it is separated from the others.

Candidates are library families trained here (``gp``, ``mlp_ensemble``, ``quadratic``) and/or models that already
exist (``pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model_source`` predictors: zoo, exported, TorchScript, callables), evaluated on
the same points. Protocol, recorded in the result:

* data: a Sobol design over a tool (a fresh design per seed) or a table (a fresh split per seed); every candidate of a
  seed sees the same training rows and the same test points;
* metrics per candidate and seed: relative RMSE and max error on the test points (inside the box), the same on an
  extrapolation set ``extrapolate`` beyond the box (tools only), interval coverage when the model gives one, fit and
  prediction time;
* ranking: test squared errors pooled over seeds; for the best candidate against each other one, a paired bootstrap
  of the mean difference; the best is the winner only when every 95 % interval excludes zero, otherwise the tied
  candidates are named.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.deploy
children.doc:
A surrogate made smaller for deployment, with both numbers measured: error lost and latency gained (#112).

"The model is smaller" is not a result. A deployment change costs accuracy and buys speed, and neither side of that
trade is worth believing unless it is measured on the same inputs and reported together — which is what every
function here returns: a :class:`DeploymentReport` carrying the relative L2 the compression cost, the p50 latency
before and after, the bytes before and after, and whether the error stayed inside the tolerance the caller set.

The paths, and the reason each is where it is:

``onnx-int8`` (:func:`compress_onnx_int8`) — **runs on any CPU.**
    The model is exported to ONNX (with a dynamic batch axis, so one graph serves a row or a batch) and quantized
    with ONNX Runtime's dynamic int8 pass: weights become int8, activations are quantized at run time, and the
    arithmetic is int8 where the kernel exists. It needs the ``onnx`` and ``onnxruntime`` extras and no GPU.

    **Where the gain is, measured:** int8 wins on *batched* inference and loses on a single row, because the
    quantize/dequantize of the activations is per call. On the 16→256→256→8 stack of the test, one thread: batch 1
    is 0.90x (slower), batch 8 is 1.45x, batch 4000 is 1.74x. The report therefore records the batch it measured —
    a "3x faster" claim with the batch hidden is exactly the kind of number this module exists to prevent — and the
    single-row latency goes in ``details`` so the losing side is visible too.

``structured-prune`` (:func:`prune_structured`, :func:`measure_pruned`) — **needs nothing but torch.**
    Whole hidden units whose incoming and outgoing weights are small are removed from a feed-forward stack, so the
    dense matrices really do get smaller — unlike magnitude pruning of individual weights, which leaves the latency
    exactly where it was. Also measured, also against the tolerance, and the numbers say what a reader needs to
    know before choosing it: on the trained 16→64→64→8 stack of the test, keeping 95 % of the units costs 11.6 %
    relative L2 for 1.16x, and keeping 50 % costs 81 % for 2.15x (50 000 rows). **Pruning without fine-tuning is
    not a deployment path on a surrogate this size** — it is fast and it destroys the answer — so the report's
    ``within_tolerance`` is False at any tolerance a surrogate would be deployed under, and that verdict is the
    deliverable, not a footnote.

``torch-int8`` (:func:`quantize_torch_dynamic`, :func:`measure_torch_dynamic`) — **works, and does not pay off here.**
    PyTorch's dynamic int8 runs once a quantized engine is selected — the macOS arm64 wheel ships ``qnnpack`` but
    leaves the engine unset, so the first call raises ``NoQEngine`` until it is set, which
    :func:`quantize_torch_dynamic` does. Measured on the same stack: relative L2 1.5 % (inside tolerance) and
    **0.88x** — *slower* than float32, because the per-call quantize/dequantize costs more than the int8 GEMM
    saves at this size. The number is reported as measured; a path that is available is not the same as a path that
    is worth taking, and this module is built so that the difference is visible.

``TensorRT`` — **declared, not executed.**
    :func:`tensorrt_status` says whether a TensorRT runtime and a CUDA device are present. There is no NVIDIA GPU
    here, so the TensorRT path is not taken and the report says so in ``tensorrt`` rather than leaving a gap a
    reader would take for an omission. The CPU number above is what a reader can reproduce.

classes.name: DeploymentReport
classes.doc: One compression, measured: what it cost in accuracy and what it bought in latency and size.

methods.doc: How many times faster the compressed model is, p50 against p50, same backend, same inputs.

methods.doc: How many times smaller, in bytes on disk — ``nan`` when the two are not comparable (see the notes).

functions.doc: Which compression paths this environment can take, and the sentence for each one it cannot.

functions.name: compress_onnx_int8
functions.sig: (module: Any, example: Any, *, n_rows: int = 4000, tolerance: float = DEFAULT_TOLERANCE, out_dir: str | Path | None = None, timing_runs: int = 20) -> DeploymentReport
functions.doc:
Export, quantize with ONNX Runtime's dynamic int8, and measure both sides of the trade.

``example`` is one input row (or a batch); ``n_rows`` rows are sampled from it for the error and the timings.
The two sessions share the backend and the input, so the latency comparison is not "ONNX against torch" but
"the same graph, int8 weights against float32 weights" — the difference a deployment would actually see.

Raises :class:`CompressionUnavailable` when the extras are missing, and nothing is written when ``out_dir`` is
None (a temporary directory is used and removed).

functions.name: prune_structured
functions.sig: (module: Any, keep: float = 0.5) -> Any
functions.doc:
Drop the least important hidden units of a feed-forward stack, keeping ``keep`` of them.

Importance is the product of the incoming and outgoing weight norms of a unit — a unit that is small on both
sides is the one that costs latency and contributes least. Only the ``out_features`` dimension of a ``Linear``
that feeds another ``Linear`` (with an activation in between) is pruned, so the next layer's ``in_features`` is
reduced with it: the dense matrices really shrink, which is the only reason latency would move at all.

Raises ``ValueError`` for a model that is not a stack of ``Linear`` layers — a convolution, a residual block or
an operator with a custom forward has no "hidden unit" this can remove without changing what it computes.

functions.sig: (module: Any, pruned: Any, example: Any, *, n_rows: int = 4000, tolerance: float = DEFAULT_TOLERANCE, timing_runs: int = 25) -> DeploymentReport
functions.doc: The pruning, measured against the model it came from: error on the same rows, p50 latency on each.

functions.name: quantize_torch_dynamic
functions.sig: (module: Any) -> Any
functions.doc:
``torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic`` on the Linear layers, with a quantized engine selected first.

The wheel ships ``qnnpack`` (or ``fbgemm``) but leaves ``torch.backends.quantized.engine`` unset, and
``quantize_dynamic`` then raises ``NoQEngine`` — which reads like "unsupported" when it is only "not
selected". The engine is set here, and only when it is unset, so a caller that chose one keeps it.

Raises :class:`CompressionUnavailable` when the build really has no quantized engine.

functions.doc: Torch's dynamic int8, measured against the float model it came from: same rows, error and p50 both.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.examples
children.doc:
Example surrogate datasets that need no download.

``airfoil_rans``  the zoo dataset ``airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6``: OpenFOAM RANS (k-omega SST, Re = 4e6) of CST airfoils;
                  inputs the six CST coefficients and the angle of attack, outputs Cl and Cd (Cm is not recorded);
                  group = the shape (whole airfoils can be held out). Its train and test splits are pooled (the
                  study re-splits); unsteady runs of the train split, recorded at the final iteration rather than
                  time-averaged, are left out.
``burgers_fields`` viscous Burgers ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on x in [-1, 1], u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x), u(+-1, t) = 0,
                  solved exactly (Cole-Hopf, Gauss-Hermite quadrature: ``pinneapple_physics.closed_form.burgers``)
                  for ``n`` viscosities log-uniform in ``nu_range``; output the field u(x, t) on an ``nx`` x ``nt``
                  grid, t in [0, t_max]. Small viscosities form a steep front at x = 0 (a near-discontinuity); the
                  recommended shift split holds out the smallest viscosities.
``cantilever_3d``  the 3-D solid FEM cantilever of the ROM Lab (``apps/rom_lab/examples/cantilever_designs.npz``: 100
                  Latin-hypercube designs over height H, width W and load angle) as a field dataset on its
                  31 x 4 x 7 node lattice: displacement (ux, uy, uz, mm) and von Mises stress (MPa). The FEM solve
                  time is measured here, on this machine, by solving ``n_timed`` stored designs again (and checking
                  that they reproduce the stored fields). The shift split holds out the smallest load angles.
                  The von Mises stress is declared non-negative (``meta["nonnegative"]``): the study trains on
                  its square root and predicts its square.

A numerical-solver baseline for ``burgers_fields``: the library's explicit upwind/FTCS finite-difference
scheme (``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.fdm``) on ``nx`` points with a stable time step, interpolated
to the dataset grid. Returns ``solve(X, coords) -> (n, n_points)``; its error against the exact solution and its
cost per query are what a surrogate competes with.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.geometry
children.doc:
Geometry-agnostic field surrogates: one interface for the models that learn on the geometry itself (#293).

The families that dominate the recent benchmarks — Transolver, GINO, the PointNet/RegDGCNN baselines, MeshGraphNet —
all take a discretised shape and return a field on it, and every one of them was written with its own input
convention. A study that wants to compare them ends up comparing the plumbing. This module fixes the plumbing once:

    sample  = GeometrySample(points, normals, conditions, fields, integrals)   # one simulation, reduced to its surface
    model   = build_geometry_surrogate("transolver")                          # one family, chosen by name
    history = model.fit(samples)                                              # train, whatever the family
    pred    = model.predict(points, normals, conditions)                      # -> fields + integrals
    report  = model.evaluate(held_out)                                        # -> relative L2, integral error, R²

Three decisions carry the interface:

- **A sample is a point set, not a grid.** The points may be any number, in any order, with any connectivity: the
  field is defined *at the points handed in*, and the same weights answer for a different count. That is what makes
  the model geometry-agnostic rather than a fixed-topology grid model.
- **The integrals are integrated from the predicted field**, by an ``integrate`` callable the case supplies, not by a
  second head. So a predicted drag can never disagree with the pressure field it came from; if the field is wrong, the
  integral is wrong in the same direction, which is the honest coupling.
- **A family that is not here says so, with the reason.** :data:`FAMILIES` lists every family the issue names:
  the implemented ones, and the open ones with the paper, the licence and what it would take — a caller reading the
  list never mistakes a stand-in for a model that is not there.

What is implemented and measured: ``transolver`` (Wu et al., ICML 2024 — physics-attention over learned slices, the
strong family on the car benchmarks) and ``pointnet`` (Qi et al., CVPR 2017 — shared MLP plus a global max pool, the
cheap baseline that is hard to beat on integrated quantities). ``gino`` and the ``meshgraphnet`` baseline are named
below, with what each would take.

The measured number, on the panel-method family of ``benchmarks/geometry_surrogate_interface.py``, is in
``benchmarks/_out/geometry_surrogate_interface.json`` and on ``docs/guides/geometry_surrogate_families.md``.

classes.name: GeometrySample
classes.doc:
One simulation reduced to its surface: points, the field on them, and the integrated quantities.

``points`` is ``(N, 3)`` and the fields are per point (``(N,)`` or ``(N, C)``), keyed by name. ``normals`` and
``elements`` are optional per-point extras the model and the integrator may use (a surface normal, a panel length,
a thickness); ``conditions`` is the global state of the run (angle of attack, Reynolds number) as scalars, given to
every point. ``integrals`` holds the quantities the simulation reported for the whole body — the target of the
integrals the model reconstructs from its own field.

methods.name: subset
methods.doc: The same sample on a subset of its points (subsampling for a batch, or a decimated surface).

classes.name: GeometryPrediction
classes.doc: What a surrogate answers for one geometry: the field at every point given, and the integrals from it.

classes.name: GeometryEvaluation
classes.doc:
The measured error of a surrogate on held-out samples, per sample and summarised.

``relative_l2`` is the field error against the simulation (the benchmark convention), ``integral_error`` the
absolute error of each integral, and ``rank_r2`` how well the model preserves the ordering of the designs by the
first integral — a field error that does not reorder the designs costs nothing at the decision level.

classes.name: GeometryFamily
classes.doc: One family in the catalogue: what it is, whether it can be built here, and what it would take if not.

classes.name: GeometrySurrogate
classes.sig: (*, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, hidden: int = 128, depth: int = 4, device: str | None = None, integrate: Callable[..., dict[str, float]] | None = None, use_normals: bool = True, seed: int = 0)
classes.doc:
The interface every geometry-agnostic surrogate implements: ``fit``, ``predict``, ``evaluate``.

A subclass provides ``_module`` (an ``nn.Module`` mapping ``(B, N, in_dim) -> (B, N, out_dim)``) and inherits the
rest: feature construction from points/normals/conditions, normalisation, subsampling for the batch, the training
loop, prediction at any point count, and the evaluation against held-out simulations.

methods.name: in_dim
methods.doc: Columns the model sees per point: the coordinates, the normals when used, the conditions broadcast.

methods.name: features
methods.doc: The model's input for one sample: coordinates, optional normals, and the conditions broadcast per point.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (samples: Iterable[GeometrySample], *, epochs: int = 60, batch: int = 8, lr: float = 0.002, n_points: int | None = None, weight_decay: float = 0.0001, seed: int | None = None, verbose: bool = False) -> GeometrySurrogate
methods.doc: Train on simulations with different geometries, point counts and conditions.

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (points: Any, normals: Any = None, conditions: dict[str, float] | None = None, elements: dict[str, Any] | None = None, *, chunk: int = 200000) -> GeometryPrediction
methods.doc: The field at the points handed in — any number of them, in any order — and the integrals from it.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc: Relative L2 of the field, the integral error and the ranking R², on simulations the model never saw.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Weights plus everything the input convention needs, so a reload predicts the same numbers.

classes.name: TransolverGeometry
classes.sig: (*, slices: int = 32, heads: int = 8, **kwargs)
classes.doc:
Transolver behind the interface (Wu et al., ICML 2024): physics-attention over learned slices.

The slices are what make it affordable on a car: attention runs among ``slices`` tokens, not among the points, so
the cost is linear in the point count. ``hidden``/``depth``/``slices`` are the capacity knobs.

classes.name: PointNetGeometry
classes.doc: PointNet behind the interface (Qi et al., CVPR 2017): the baseline without geometric attention.

functions.name: available_families
functions.sig: (*, implemented_only: bool = False) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc: The catalogue as data: every family the issue names, with whether it is here and why not.

functions.name: build_geometry_surrogate
functions.sig: (family: str = 'transolver', **kwargs) -> GeometrySurrogate
functions.doc: The family by name, or ``ValueError`` naming the ones that exist and the reason the requested one is open.

functions.name: samples_from_panel
functions.sig: (shapes: Sequence[Any], *, alphas: Sequence[float] = (4.0,), n_per_side: int = 60, field: str = 'cp') -> list[GeometrySample]
functions.doc:
The panel-method family as ``GeometrySample``s: a 2-D body lifted to a surface point set and labelled by the
Hess-Smith solver the library already uses as its inviscid reference.

Each sample carries the point set (``x, y, 0``), the outward normal of every panel, the panel length in
``elements`` (the integrator needs it), the angle of attack as a condition, and ``cp`` on every point plus ``cl``
and ``cd`` as integrals. This is the small real case the interface is measured on — a real solver, real bodies,
and a point count that is not the same for every shape once ``n_per_side`` or the geometry changes.

functions.name: panel_integrals
functions.sig: (*, fields: dict[str, np.ndarray], normals: np.ndarray, elements: dict[str, np.ndarray], conditions: dict[str, float], **_) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
``integrate`` for the panel family: the solver's own pressure integration, applied to the predicted field.

Force per unit dynamic pressure on a panel is ``-(Cp n L)``; resolved onto the free-stream axes it gives the lift
and drag coefficients. The same formula ``benchmarks/geometry_conditioned_surrogate.lift_from_cp`` uses, so a
predicted Cl is the integral of the predicted Cp and the two can never disagree.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.heldout
children.doc:
Held-out errors of a field surrogate trained on snapshots (``data.from_snapshots``), in the terms of the snapshots:
per field over all held-out samples, per region of the body, and on the scalar quantities an engineer reads off the
field (the largest displacement at a loaded face, the largest stress).

    from pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.heldout import heldout_report
    rep = heldout_report(snaps, data, model, st.splits.test)
    rep["fields"]["von_mises"]["rel_l2"], rep["fields"]["von_mises"]["regions"], rep["qois"]

Every number compares the model's prediction at a held-out sample's parameters with the stored full-order result.

functions.name: region_rel_l2
functions.sig: (pred, true, regions: dict[str, Sequence[int]]) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Relative L2 error restricted to each region's points, over all samples: ``pred``/``true`` (n, m) or
(n, m, components) with the points on axis 1.

functions.name: heldout_report
functions.sig: (snaps, data: SurrogateData, model, idx, *, grow: float = 0.1) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Errors of ``model`` (a ``SurrogateModel`` or anything with ``predict_array``) on the samples ``idx``:
``fields`` (relative L2 over all of them, per region: the dataset's node sets grown by ``grow`` times the body,
see ``rom.views.zones``; ``per_sample``: the mean and median of the per-sample errors and the share of the pooled
weight, the squared field, that the ``heaviest`` samples hold), ``qois`` (per sample, true and predicted: the largest magnitude of each vector field on
each node set, the largest value of each scalar field) and ``samples`` (relative L2 per sample and field). Fields
declared non-negative (``data.meta["nonnegative"]``, e.g. a von Mises stress) also count the predicted values
below zero, which are physically invalid: ``fields[name]["negative_values"]`` and per sample
``negative_<name>``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.limits
children.doc:
Where a surrogate may be used: validity bounds, an out-of-distribution gate, and where its errors concentrate.

``OODGate`` is the batched form of ``pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.Envelope`` (same rule, vectorised): a query is out of distribution when an input is
outside the training range, or when its nearest training sample is farther than ``knn_limit`` times the typical
training spacing (standardised inputs, log10 for positive inputs), i.e. inside the box but in a hole of the data.

``limitations`` measures, on held-out samples only: the error inside and outside the gate, the error per input
quartile (where the error concentrates), the worst samples, the extrapolation ratio (shift error / test error) and,
for fields, where on the grid the error is largest.

classes.name: OODGate
classes.sig: (X_train: np.ndarray, names: Sequence[str], knn_limit: float = 3.0)

methods.name: assess
methods.doc: Per row: ``ood``, inputs ``outside`` the range, ``knn_distance`` (x typical spacing), ``reasons``.

functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, true: np.ndarray, scale: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Per sample: RMS over outputs of (pred - true) / scale (``scale``: per-output std of the training targets; for
fields the per-sample relative L2 is used instead, see ``study``).

functions.name: limitations
functions.sig: (gate: OODGate, X_eval: np.ndarray, err: np.ndarray, sets: Mapping[str, np.ndarray], X_train: np.ndarray, *, field_err: np.ndarray | None = None, coords: np.ndarray | None = None, coord_names: Sequence[str] = (), metric: str = 'error') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``X_eval`` / ``err``: held-out samples (test and shift) and their per-sample error; ``sets``: name -> boolean
mask over them. ``field_err``: (n_eval, n_points) pointwise absolute error, for the error map.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.methods
children.doc:
Surrogate candidates: which methods apply to a dataset, and how each is trained under a ``ComputeBudget``.

==========  =====================================================  ===========================================
id           method                                                 applies to
==========  =====================================================  ===========================================
ridge        quadratic-polynomial ridge regression (scikit-learn)   scalars, fields (classical baseline)
gp           Gaussian process, Matern-5/2 ARD + noise; fields on    up to ``GP_MAX_N`` training samples
             POD coefficients (scikit-learn)
gbt          gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost if installed, else     scalars
             scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting)
mlp          multilayer perceptron (PyTorch)                        scalars, fields (all grid points as outputs)
fno          Fourier neural operator, parameters as constant        fields on a 1-D or 2-D uniform grid
             input channels (``pinneapple_neural``)
deeponet     DeepONet, branch = parameters, trunk = coordinates     fields
             (``pinneapple_neural``)
pinn         physics-informed MLP u(parameters, coordinates):       fields with a declared PDE (``pde.py``)
             data loss + PDE residual
==========  =====================================================  ===========================================

Every method sees the same training samples, normalisation (training split only) and validation samples. The
iterative methods (mlp, fno, deeponet, pinn) train until the same ``ComputeBudget`` is spent
(``train_within_budget``) and keep their best validation checkpoint out of ten evaluations, whose time is not
charged; the one-shot fits (ridge, gp, gbt) are fitted once and report the time they used, which can be below the
budget (they are never given more).

classes.doc: What a method gets: raw arrays (``Y`` flattened to (n, p)), training-split scalers, the field layout.

classes.name: Fitted
classes.doc: A trained candidate: ``predict(X_raw) -> Y_raw`` with ``Y`` flattened (n, p).

classes.name: NonNegative
classes.sig: (inner: Fitted, mask: np.ndarray)
classes.doc:
A candidate trained on the square root of the outputs in ``mask`` (a boolean over the flattened outputs, e.g.
a von Mises stress channel): it predicts their square, so they are never negative.

methods.name: forward_target
methods.doc: What the inner model is trained on: ``sqrt`` of the masked outputs.

functions.doc: ``{method: None if applicable else the reason it is not}`` for every registered candidate.

functions.doc: Train ``method``; returns the fitted model and the wall time of the fit (one-shot fits: the whole fit).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model
children.doc:
A trained surrogate packaged for use: predict with the OOD gate, save / load, export, model card.

``SurrogateModel.save(dir)`` writes ``model.pkl`` (the fitted candidate, pickled) and ``card.json`` (inputs,
outputs, validity bounds, OOD gate, held-out metrics, limitations, trust report, dataset hash, the model file's
sha256). ``load`` verifies that hash before unpickling. Unpickling runs code: load only models you produced
(the gateway stores the ones it publishes; it never unpickles an upload).

``export(path, "torchscript" | "onnx")`` writes a self-contained graph of the PyTorch candidates (mlp, fno,
deeponet, pinn) that takes raw inputs ``(n, d)`` and returns raw outputs ``(n, p)`` (normalisation included); the
scikit-learn and XGBoost candidates have no such export here.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model_source
children.doc:
Use a model already trained instead of training one (#1190): your own (TorchScript, ONNX, a callable, or a model
exported by :mod:`.workflow`), one from the PINNeAPPle zoo, or train one. Every model passes an applicability gate
before it is used, forward or inverse, and the result is re-verified by the solver when there is one.

* :func:`zoo_candidates` ranks the zoo's models for a problem by the outputs it needs and the inputs it has (names,
  then units), with what is missing.
* :func:`open_model` gives one :class:`Predictor` (inputs, outputs, units, bounds, ``predict``) whatever the source.
* :func:`gate` before use: the query inside the model's validity box (and its extra constraints), the problem's
  units convertible to the model's, and a check against references: the zoo's stored reference (its card's
  metrics recomputed) or a few solves of the reference tool, with the error against the model's claimed accuracy.
* :func:`use_model` runs it forward at the query points or inverse (the parameters that reproduce observations,
  bounded least squares through the model), then re-verifies with the solver when one is given.

classes.name: Predictor
fields: extra_mask: Callable[[Mapping[str, np.ndarray]], np.ndarray] | None = None

functions.name: zoo_candidates
functions.sig: (outputs: Sequence[str], inputs: Sequence[str] = (), units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Zoo models ranked for a problem: outputs matched (by name, or by unit when ``units`` names them), inputs the
problem lacks; best first.

functions.name: open_model
functions.sig: (source: str, *, path: str | None = None, name: str | None = None, fn: Callable | None = None, inputs: Sequence[str] = (), outputs: Sequence[str] = (), bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, claimed_rel_error: float | None = None) -> Predictor
functions.doc:
One predictor from ``source``: ``"zoo"`` (``name``), ``"workflow"`` (``path`` of a model exported by
:func:`.workflow.surrogate_modeling`), ``"torchscript"`` / ``"onnx"`` (``path`` plus the declared ``inputs``,
``outputs``, ``bounds``, ``units``: a file carries no physics, so its card is the caller's), ``"callable"``
(``fn(**inputs) -> dict``).

functions.name: onnx_function
functions.sig: (path: str, inputs: Sequence[str], outputs: Sequence[str]) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
An ONNX file as ``f(X) -> Y``: ``X`` (N, len(inputs)) in the declared input order, ``Y`` (N, len(outputs))
in float64.

The file's own signature is checked against the declared card when it is opened, and a mismatch is refused with
both name lists: one input tensor needs ``len(inputs)`` columns (or one tensor per declared input, by name); one
output tensor needs ``len(outputs)`` columns (or one tensor per declared output, by name). Each input is cast to
the tensor's own element type (float64 data into a float32 model, and the reverse). A model exported with a
fixed batch dimension is run in chunks of that size (the last chunk padded and the padding dropped).

functions.sig: (p: Predictor, query: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]], *, problem_units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, reference: Callable[..., Mapping[str, float]] | None = None, n_reference: int = 8, tolerance: float | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Whether ``p`` may be used at ``query``: ``{"ok", "checks"}``. ``reference(**inputs) -> outputs`` (a solver)
is compared with the model at ``n_reference`` query points; without one, a zoo model's stored reference is
recomputed. ``tolerance``: relative error allowed (default: twice the model's claimed error, else 5 %).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.pde
children.doc:
PDE declarations for physics-informed surrogates: which residual a PINN candidate adds to its data loss.

A declaration names the equation, maps its coordinates to the field's coordinate names and its coefficients to
input columns (or constants)::

    {"type": "burgers", "coords": {"x": "x", "t": "t"}, "coefficients": {"nu": "nu"}}

Supported equations (``u`` the scalar field):

========== =============================== ==================
type        residual                        coords / coefficients
========== =============================== ==================
heat        u_t - alpha u_xx                x, t / alpha
burgers     u_t + u u_x - nu u_xx           x, t / nu
advection   u_t + c u_x                     x, t / c
poisson_1d  k u_xx + f                      x / k, f
laplace_2d  u_xx + u_yy                     x, y / -
========== =============================== ==================

The PINN candidate is only offered when a declaration is given: without a PDE there is no physics loss.

methods.name: residual
methods.doc: PDE residual at ``coords`` (n, n_coord_dims, requires_grad) for ``params`` (n, d) in physical units.

methods.name: fd_residual
methods.sig: (fields: np.ndarray, coords: np.ndarray, params: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Second-order finite-difference residual of fields ``(n, *grid)`` on a tensor-product grid (``coords``
(n_points, n_dims) in ``ij`` order), RMS per sample over the interior points. Applied to the reference data
it measures the data's own discretisation error, the floor a prediction is compared against.

functions.name: parse_pde
functions.sig: (decl: Mapping[str, Any] | None, coord_names: list[str], input_names: list[str]) -> PDEDeclaration | None

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.study
children.doc:
Surrogate study: train every applicable candidate on the same data and budget, measure on unseen data, pick one.

``run_study(data, ...)``

1. splits once (``make_splits``): train / validation / held-out test, plus a distribution-shift set never seen in
   training (whole groups, the edge of the input space, or one end of an input);
2. lists every candidate with the reason it does or does not apply (fields vs scalars; PINN only with a declared
   PDE; GP sample limit);
3. trains each applicable candidate for each seed under the same ``ComputeBudget``
   (``pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget``) and measures, in physical units, the held-out and shift errors,
   training time, inference time per query, parameter count and model size;
4. selects the method with the lowest **validation** error (the test and shift sets never choose), and packages it
   as a ``SurrogateModel`` with its limitations (validity bounds, OOD gate, where errors concentrate) and a trust
   report (``pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport``) whose checks all ran on held-out data.

Error metrics: scalars, ``nrmse`` = RMSE / standard deviation of the training targets, per output then averaged;
fields, ``rel_l2`` = ||pred - true|| / ||true|| per sample, averaged.

methods.doc: The study as a report: data, protocol, comparison, chosen model, trust checks, limitations.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.workflow
children.doc:
The standard surrogate-modeling workflow (#1186): data or a design of experiments over a tool, the model family
``recommend_architecture`` picks (or none), the library's equal-budget comparison, checks on solves never trained
on, and an exported model that refuses to extrapolate.

1. **Data**: an uploaded table (``table``: rows of inputs and outputs) or a Sobol design of experiments over a tool
   (``tool``: a callable or a library tool id, ``bounds`` per input, ``outputs`` it returns). The cost of one tool
   call is measured.
2. **Which model**: :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_recommendation.recommend_architecture` with
   the measured cost and ``n_uses`` (how many predictions the model will serve). ``none`` stops here with its
   reason: call the tool (``force=True`` trains anyway, to compare).
3. **Families on one protocol**: :func:`pinneapple_autolab.study.benchmark.benchmark` (k-fold CV on train + val,
   cross-conformal 90 % intervals, the selection rule written in the record); the GP, the MLP ensemble and the
   quadratic response surface (the baseline to beat).
4. **Checks** on ``n_fresh`` new tool calls inside the box (or the table's held-out rows): relative RMSE against
   ``accuracy_target``, coverage of the 90 % interval (binomial band at that sample size), and that the selected
   family beats the quadratic baseline.
5. **Export**: the selected models with their intervals and a model card (inputs, ranges, units, errors, checks,
   provenance); :func:`load_surrogate` returns a predictor that raises on inputs outside the trained box.

The exported predictor: ``predict({"x": .., ...}) -> {output: (mean, 90 % half width)}``; raises ValueError for
an input outside the trained box (no silent extrapolation). Load only files you produced: it is a pickle.

children.doc:
Surrogate models from simulation results: select, compare at equal budget, measure on unseen data, package.

>>> from pinneapple_analysis import surrogate
>>> data = surrogate.examples.airfoil_rans()                 # OpenFOAM RANS campaign, Cl and Cd
>>> study = surrogate.run_study(data, budget=5.0, seeds=2)   # every applicable method, same splits and budget
>>> study.best, study.ranking("test"), study.trust["decision"]
>>> study.model.predict({"T0": 0.15, ..., "alpha_deg": 4.0})  # outputs + per-row OOD assessment
>>> study.model.save("model_dir")

Modules: ``geometry`` (the geometry-agnostic families — Transolver, PointNet — behind ``fit``/``predict``),
``data`` (tables and arrays -> ``SurrogateData``), ``splits`` (held-out and distribution-shift splits),
``methods`` (ridge, gp, gbt, mlp, fno, deeponet, pinn and when each applies), ``pde`` (declared equations for the
PINN), ``limits`` (validity bounds, OOD gate, error concentration), ``model`` (``SurrogateModel``), ``study``
(``run_study``), ``examples`` (datasets that need no download), ``contracts`` (``DatasetSpec``, ``ModelRef``,
``StudyResult`` of ``pinneapple_data.contracts``; imported on use). Needs ``pip install "pinneapple[surrogate]"``
(scikit-learn; Parquet, HDF5 and ONNX support).
